operand-rendering lambdas that pick ctx-field vs local based on config flags
usage tracking (RecompilerLocalVariables) to emit only needed local decls
literal 1:1 transliteration (correctness over readability)
uniform PPC_FUNC_IMPL/PPC_FUNC_PROLOGUE wrapping per function
__restrict ctx + volatile memory to constrain the optimizer safely
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: ppu_lifter.py already does string-template emission per opcode, so the architecture matches. Concrete upgrades to steal: (1) the operand-lambda pattern that centralizes the local-vs-context decision (lets you add the localization performance optimization later without touching every opcode); (2) emitting a fixed uniform function signature/prologue macro; (3) the union views so each opcode addresses the exact width/signedness. Because the PS3 PPU ISA is a near-superset of what Xenon implements (same base PowerPC), large swaths of XenonRecomp's per-opcode emission code are reusable as a reference for correct C semantics (carry/overflow in XER, CR-field updates on dot-suffixed ops, rlwinm/rldicl mask math).

dimensions.howItWorks: VMX and VMX128 instructions are lifted to SIMD intrinsics through SIMDE (SIMD Everywhere), so the same generated code compiles to SSE on x86 and NEON on ARM64. Example: VADDFP/VADDFP128 -> `simde_mm_store_ps({d}.f32, simde_mm_add_ps(simde_mm_load_ps({a}.f32), simde_mm_load_ps({b}.f32)));`. The crucial trick: instead of byte-swapping each 32-bit lane on load/store, the recompiler stores the ENTIRE 16-byte vector register in reversed byte order. This makes vector memory loads/stores cheap but means element indices are reversed — generated code must compensate (e.g. use W,Z,Y lanes instead of X,Y,Z in dot products, and reverse operand order for pack instructions). VMX128 (the 360 extension with 128 vector registers and extra opcodes like vmx128 permute/pack variants) is handled by the same machinery as base VMX (v0..v127 in the context).
techniques: SIMDE intrinsic emission for portable SSE/NEON from one C++ source
store whole 16-byte vector reversed (avoid per-lane byteswap)
compensate lane order in generated code (WZYX vs XYZW, reversed pack args)
treat VMX128 as VMX with a larger register file + extra opcode forms
per-element-typed access via the f32[4]/u32[4]/u8[16] union views
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: Highly relevant: the PS3 PPU's VMX/AltiVec unit is essentially the same SIMD ISA family as Xenon's base VMX (vector float add/madd, perm, pack/unpack, compares, splats). ps3recomp can adopt the exact SIMDE-based emission to get x86+ARM portability for free, and must make the same byte-reversal vs lane-order decision up front (the whole-vector-reverse trick is a clean choice that keeps loads cheap at the cost of lane-index compensation). Xenon's VMX128 lane-reversal compensation table is a near-ready reference for which AltiVec ops need reversed lanes/args. SEPARATELY, the SPU's 128-bit SIMD ISA is a DIFFERENT instruction set (not AltiVec) — but the same SIMDE backend and union-vector-register approach apply; you write a new per-opcode table for SPU but reuse the codegen and endianness strategy.

dimensions.howItWorks: The generated code operates entirely on little-endian host values; byteswap is pushed into the load/store macros. PPC_LOAD_U8 = `*(volatile uint8_t*)(base+x)`; PPC_LOAD_U16/32/64 wrap the access in `__builtin_bswap16/32/64`; the STORE macros byteswap before writing back to big-endian guest memory. ALL loads/stores are marked `volatile` specifically to stop Clang from reordering/coalescing them across the implicit big-endian boundary in unsafe ways. Vectors are handled differently (whole-register reverse, see SIMD dimension). A separate PPC_MM_STORE_* path exists for the (unfinished) MMIO case. Memory itself is a single flat `uint8_t* base`; a guest pointer is just `base + guest_addr.u32` (Xbox 360 uses 32-bit guest pointers, hence base is the second arg to every function).
techniques: byteswap baked into load/store macros (not into instruction logic)
__builtin_bswap16/32/64 for the swaps
volatile-qualified guest memory access to prevent unsafe reordering
flat base+guest_addr memory model, 32-bit guest pointers
separate MMIO store path stubbed for hardware registers
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: ps3recomp already maps vm memory as host_ptr = g_base + guest_addr and converts endianness at boundaries — XenonRecomp validates this exact design and adds two concrete lessons: (1) mark guest memory access volatile to prevent the optimizer from breaking big-endian semantics (a subtle correctness trap that can cause non-deterministic boot failures); (2) keep the swap in the macro layer so the per-opcode lifter stays endianness-agnostic. PS3 PPU is 64-bit so guest pointers are wider, but the model is identical. For SPU, local store is internally addressed and the DMA/MFC engine does the big-endian main-memory transfers, so the byteswap belongs in the MFC DMA implementation, not in every SPU load/store.

dimensions.dimension: Indirect branches, link register, mtctr/bctr, returns
dimensions.howItWorks: Direct calls: BL emits `ctx.lr = 0x<next>;` (skipped if skip_lr) then a direct C++ call `targetFunc(ctx, base);`. Returns: BLR emits plain `return;` (the C++ call stack replaces the guest LR chain). Intra-function unconditional branch B -> `goto loc_<target>;`. The link register is treated as redundant for control flow because recompilation already encodes returns as C returns — skip_lr can drop LR maintenance entirely UNLESS the game inspects LR or uses C++ exceptions. CTR: MTCTR copies into ctx.ctr (or a local). BCTR: if a switch table is registered for that address, emit a real `switch`/`goto`; otherwise it is an indirect call/jump resolved at runtime via PPC_CALL_INDIRECT_FUNC(addr). Indirect/virtual calls go through PPC_LOOKUP_FUNC: a 'perfect hash' function-pointer table where the recompiled-function pointer is found by dereferencing `*(PPCFunc**)(base + guest_addr*2 + ...)`. The table lives in guest memory space placed just past the valid XEX region in the base allocation (an earlier design used a full 8 GB sparse virtual allocation but that caused too much memory pressure).
techniques: guest call -> direct C++ call; guest return (blr) -> C return (host stack is the call stack)
skip_lr optimization: drop LR bookkeeping unless LR is read or exceptions used
bctr -> native switch when a table is known, else runtime indirect lookup
PPC_LOOKUP_FUNC perfect-hash: address*2 indexes a function-pointer table
function-pointer table stored just past the XEX region in the base allocation (avoids 8GB sparse map)
tail-call-shaped branches recompiled as calls (cf. N64Recomp)
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: This is the core answer to ps3recomp's 'function pointers / vtables / switch tables hard to resolve' gap. (1) Model returns as native C returns and only keep LR when needed — cheap and removes a whole class of state. (2) For PS3 PPU's mtctr/bctr / bctrl (vtable dispatch, function pointers), build the same address-keyed function-pointer table in the runtime so any computed target resolves at runtime even when static analysis can't name it — this is the pragmatic escape from the static-resolution wall. (3) Place that table inside the guest address space past the loaded image to avoid huge sparse allocations. (4) For SPU, the analog is bi/bisl/bisled (branch-indirect via register) which dispatch through computed local-store addresses — a per-SPU-context function-pointer table indexed by local-store address gives the same runtime fallback, important because SPU overlays mean targets are often unknowable statically.

dimensions.dimension: FPU vs VMX denormal/rounding state (CSR state machine)
dimensions.howItWorks: The PPC FPU must leave denormals intact, but VMX always flushes denormals to zero — conflicting host FPU modes. XenonRecomp stores the float control word in ctx.fpscr.csr and toggles flush mode around instruction groups. To avoid emitting a mode-switch before every instruction, the recompiler keeps a COMPILE-TIME `enum class CSRState { Unknown, FPU, VMX }` and a printSetFlushMode(enable) lambda: it only emits `ctx.fpscr.enableFlushMode()` / `disableFlushMode()` when the tracked csrState differs from the needed one, and appends an 'Unconditional' suffix when transitioning out of Unknown. Consecutive VMX instructions thus pay the mode switch once, not per instruction. The state resets at block/call boundaries where it can't be proven.
techniques: model FPSCR as host MXCSR/FPCR control word
compile-time CSRState tracking to elide redundant rounding/flush-mode writes
emit flush-mode toggle only on FPU<->VMX transitions
Unconditional-suffix variant for the first set from Unknown state
reset state at control-flow merges to stay correct
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: Directly applicable to the PS3 PPU, which has the identical FPU-keeps-denormals vs VMX/AltiVec-flushes-denormals conflict (AltiVec runs in non-Java/flush mode). Adopting the compile-time CSRState elision in ppu_lifter.py gives both correctness (matching denormal behavior, which affects physics/audio determinism) and performance (avoids a costly MXCSR write per instruction). This is a non-obvious, high-value optimization that a naive lifter would miss, and it is one of the subtler bugs to get right when a game finally boots.

dimensions.dimension: Guest<->host trampolines / HLE / kernel imports (NID analog)
dimensions.howItWorks: In UnleashedRecomp (the runtime), imported Xbox kernel/XAM functions are HLE'd in C++ and bound with `GUEST_FUNCTION_HOOK(__imp__KeSetEvent, KeSetEvent)`, which expands to `PPC_FUNC(__imp__KeSetEvent){ HostToGuestFunction<KeSetEvent>(ctx, base); }`. GUEST_FUNCTION_STUB(sym) expands to an empty PPC_FUNC for ignorable imports. The recompiler emits the guest import thunk as a weak `__imp__<name>` symbol; the hook provides the strong definition, so the linker resolves guest import calls straight to host code (no per-call dispatch). HostToGuestFunction marshals PPC registers -> native C++ args: ArgTranslator reads integer/pointer args from r3..r10 (then stack) and FP args from f1..f13, dispatching via type traits (GetIntegerArgumentValue / GetPrecisionArgumentValue), runs the native function, and writes the return value back to r3 (ints/pointers) or f1 (floats). GuestToHostFunction is the inverse (host calls into guest code: pack native args into a PPCContext, invoke the recompiled guest function, read result from r3/f1) — used for callbacks and re-entering guest code. The whole thing respects the PPC System V ABI (r1 stack pointer, FPSCR preserved across the boundary).
techniques: weak __imp__<name> symbol from recompiler + strong host definition = linker-resolved HLE
GUEST_FUNCTION_HOOK / GUEST_FUNCTION_STUB macros to declare HLE bindings
HostToGuestFunction: template arg-marshal r3..r10/f1..f13 -> native call -> r3/f1
GuestToHostFunction: native -> PPC context -> guest call -> read r3/f1 (callbacks)
ArgTranslator with type-trait dispatch for int vs float vs stack-overflow args
PPC System V ABI compliance (r1, FPSCR, return regs) at the boundary
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: This is the model for ps3recomp's HLE/NID layer. PS3 imports are resolved by 32-bit NID = first 4 bytes of SHA1(name); ps3recomp can emit a weak `__imp__nid_<HEX>` (or by resolved name) symbol per import stub and let HLE libs provide strong definitions via a PS3 analog of GUEST_FUNCTION_HOOK — turning NID resolution into ordinary link-time symbol resolution instead of a runtime dispatch table. The HostToGuestFunction/GuestToHostFunction/ArgTranslator templates map almost directly onto the PS3 PPU PPC64 ELFv1 ABI (args in r3..r10, FP in f1..f13, return in r3/f1, descriptor-based calls via .opd) and are exactly what's needed for LV2 syscalls and cellXxx callbacks that re-enter guest code (e.g. cellGcmSys flip callbacks, thread entry points). The macro/template pattern also gives an easy 'stub it' path (GUEST_FUNCTION_STUB) for the many cell functions that can be no-ops early on.

dimensions.dimension: Runtime / memory model / setjmp-longjmp / context size
dimensions.howItWorks: XenonRecomp itself provides NO runtime — making the game run is the integrator's job (UnleashedRecomp is that runtime for one title). Memory is the flat base allocation; guest pointers are base-relative. setjmp/longjmp are NOT recompiled instruction-by-instruction (the saved register set would be wrong) — instead the config supplies their guest addresses and the recompiler redirects them to native implementations; importantly the PPCContext is made large enough to also hold a host jmp_buf / x86 (and other arch) CPU state so native setjmp/longjmp can save/restore through the same struct. Heap, threads (ExCreateThread), events, critical sections, file I/O, signin/video are all HLE in the runtime's kernel/ layer (imports.cpp, heap.cpp, memory.cpp, xam.cpp). MMIO (e.g. XMA audio decode registers) is acknowledged as currently unimplemented and noted as non-trivial.
techniques: recompiler = pure code translator; runtime is a separate, swappable layer
setjmp/longjmp redirected to native impls via config addresses (not lifted)
oversize guest context to embed host jmp_buf / native CPU state
HLE kernel layer (heap/memory/threads/events/io/xam) as plain C++
MMIO left as an explicit, acknowledged gap
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: Validates ps3recomp's architecture (separate runtime, flat mapped memory, LV2 syscalls + HLE libs). Two concrete lessons: (1) Do NOT try to statically lift setjmp/longjmp (or PS3's sys_ppu_thread context save) instruction-by-instruction; detect them and redirect to native versions, and size ppu_context to hold a host jmp_buf so native long jumps work — directly relevant since PS3 newlib/EH uses setjmp/longjmp. (2) Treat hardware-register/MMIO-style access (and the RSX register pokes) as a known hard gap to be HLE'd at a higher semantic level rather than emulated at the bus level. For SPU, the runtime must additionally model 256KB local store, MFC DMA queues, and mailbox/channel ops as a host-side library — analogous to UnleashedRecomp's kernel/ layer but per-SPU-context.

dimensions.howItWorks: XenosRecomp is a SEPARATE tool that statically recompiles Xbox 360 Xenos shader microcode into HLSL, which is then compiled to DXIL (D3D12) and SPIR-V (Vulkan) via DXC. It parses the Xenos shader container (constant-buffer reflection, interpolators, vertex declarations, instruction stream), converts vector/ALU ops directly, and — because HLSL has no goto — reconstructs control flow as a `while(true){ switch(pc){ ... } }` loop with a software program-counter selecting blocks. UnleashedRecomp does NOT emulate the Xenos GPU; it implements a translation layer (renderer) on top of 'plume', a rendering hardware abstraction layer over D3D12/Vulkan. Pipeline/shader compilation is integrated into the game's asset-loading path and the converted shaders ship as a precompiled DXIL/SPIR-V cache.
techniques: static shader-microcode -> HLSL -> DXIL/SPIR-V via DXC (AOT, cached)
control flow without goto: while+switch on a software PC
parse shader container metadata (CBs, interpolators, vertex decls) for reflection
translation-layer renderer (plume HAL over D3D12/Vulkan), not GPU emulation
shaders baked into the asset pipeline as a precompiled cache
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: Directly inspirational for the RSX path. ps3recomp currently parses the RSX NV47 FIFO command stream via cellGcmSys HLE into a backend (null/D3D12, Vulkan planned) — the translation-layer (not GPU-emulation) philosophy matches XenosRecomp/plume exactly and is the right call. The transferable idea: RSX vertex/fragment programs (NV40-class microcode) can be STATICALLY recompiled to HLSL/SPIR-V the same way Xenos microcode is, and cached, instead of being JIT-translated per draw. The while+switch-on-PC pattern is the standard trick for lowering microcode control flow into shading languages that lack goto. The plume-style HAL is a good model for the planned multi-backend (D3D12 + Vulkan) RSX renderer.

dimensions.dimension: Modding / patching / function replacement (prior art from N64Recomp)
dimensions.howItWorks: The lineage tool N64Recomp (which inspired XenonRecomp) supports function-level patching via link order: it can emit single-file output, and 'providing the recompiled patches to the linker before the original recompiler output results in the patches taking priority over functions with the same names.' RecompModTool packages mods; the TOML can stub functions, skip recompilation of specific functions, or patch single instructions in the target binary. N64Recomp lifts indirect jumps as `LOOKUP_FUNC(ctx->r25)(rdram, ctx)` and recompiles tail-call-shaped branches into real calls. XenonRecomp inherits the same philosophy (literal transliteration, context struct, LOOKUP_FUNC-style indirect resolution) and UnleashedRecomp adds Hedge Mod Manager / Sonic-Generations-format mod compatibility on top.
techniques: weak-symbol / link-order override to replace recompiled functions with hand-written ones
TOML-driven function stubbing, skip, and single-instruction patching
single-file output mode to make symbol-level override practical
tail-call detection -> emit as C call (clean stacks, enables override)
ship mods as native code linked against the same context ABI
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: Gives ps3recomp a pragmatic strategy for the ~28% of functions it can't lift correctly and for incremental bring-up: emit each guest function as a weakly-linked symbol so a hand-written native replacement (or HLE shim) can override it just by linking first. This converts 'static recompilation must be perfect' into 'recompile what you can, hand-patch the rest' — exactly the workflow needed since no PS3 game has booted end-to-end yet. Single-instruction patching and per-function stub/skip in the config let you neutralize problematic routines (e.g. a copy-protection check, or a function that touches un-emulated MMIO) without blocking the whole build. The same mechanism doubles as the eventual modding story.

dimensions.howItWorks: The repo includes a XenonTests project dedicated to validating PPC instruction implementations (the README ties Clang 18+ correctness to instruction intrinsics). The recompiler emits per-function C++ across multiple split files (cppFileIndex sharding) so the huge generated translation unit set compiles in parallel and within compiler limits. invalid_instructions config entries keep known non-code (padding, frame handlers) from being lifted and breaking the build.
techniques: dedicated instruction-semantics test suite (XenonTests)
split generated output across many .cpp files for parallel/feasible compilation
invalid_instructions carve-outs to keep the generated TU compilable
Clang-targeted codegen (relies on __builtin_* and intrinsic behavior)
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: ps3recomp should build a per-opcode semantics test harness (compare lifted-C output vs a reference PPU/SPU interpreter on randomized inputs) — the cheapest way to raise confidence in carry/overflow/CR/denormal edge cases before any game boots. The output-sharding lesson matters at PS3 scale: a full title is huge, so split generated C across many files (the project's docs already imply large function counts) for tractable MSVC/GCC/Clang builds. The invalid_instructions carve-out concept prevents data/literal pools and switch tables (which the find_functions recall gap can misclassify) from poisoning the compile.

standoutInnovations: Whole-vector byte-reversal: store the entire 16-byte VMX register reversed in memory (instead of per-lane byteswap on each load/store) and compensate lane order in generated code (WZY instead of XYZ, reversed pack args). Cheap big-endian vector memory at the cost of a fixed, mechanical lane-index remap — directly applicable to PS3 PPU AltiVec.

Compile-time CSRState (Unknown/FPU/VMX) machine that emits an MXCSR/FPCR flush-mode toggle ONLY on FPU<->VMX transitions, collapsing a per-instruction rounding-mode write into one-per-run. Solves the FPU-keeps-denormals vs VMX-flushes-denormals conflict that the PS3 PPU shares, with both correctness and speed benefits.

Jump-table recovery by opcode-sequence masks + backward cmplwi scan + literal-table read, emitted as a side-channel TOML the recompiler turns into native switch/goto. A clean separation that also lets humans hand-add tables the matcher misses — the most directly stealable fix for ps3recomp's indirect-branch gap.

Runtime 'perfect hash' function-pointer table keyed by guest address (address*2 index), placed just past the loaded image inside the base allocation, so any computed/indirect target resolves at runtime even when static analysis can't name it — the pragmatic escape from the static-resolution wall (and they abandoned an 8GB sparse-map design for this).

Weak __imp__<name> symbols emitted by the recompiler + strong host definitions via GUEST_FUNCTION_HOOK turn HLE/import resolution into plain link-time symbol resolution (no runtime dispatch). With HostToGuestFunction/GuestToHostFunction/ArgTranslator marshalling r3..r10/f1..f13, this is a near-drop-in model for PS3 NID->host binding and LV2 syscalls/callbacks.

Don't lift setjmp/longjmp instruction-by-instruction: detect them by config address, redirect to native impls, and oversize the guest context struct so it can hold a host jmp_buf / native CPU state. Same trick handles save/restore millicode helpers via byte signatures.

Treat recompilation output as overridable: weak-symbol/link-order function replacement (from N64Recomp) plus per-function stub/skip and single-instruction patches in config — enabling 'recompile what you can, hand-patch the rest', the realistic path to a first boot.

Static shader recompilation (XenosRecomp): microcode -> HLSL -> DXIL/SPIR-V cached AOT, with goto-free control flow lowered to while(true){switch(pc)} — the model for statically recompiling RSX NV40-class vertex/fragment programs instead of JITing them.
verifiableClaims: XenonAnalyse detects switch/jump tables by matching exactly four opcode-sequence masks (SWITCH_ABSOLUTE = LIS,ADDI,RLWINM,LWZX,MTCTR,BCTR; plus computed, byte-offset, and short/word-offset variants) and recovers the case count by scanning backward for a cmplwi bound (labels.resize(operand+1)), emitting a TOML with [[switch]] {base, r, default, labels[]}.

Every recompiled guest function has the signature void func(PPCContext& __restrict ctx, uint8_t* base) (PPC_FUNC macro), and indirect calls resolve via PPC_LOOKUP_FUNC dereferencing a function-pointer table indexed by guest address*2, stored just past the XEX region in the base allocation (replacing an earlier 8GB sparse virtual allocation).

Memory loads/stores byteswap via __builtin_bswap16/32/64 inside PPC_LOAD_*/PPC_STORE_* macros and are volatile-qualified specifically to stop Clang from unsafe reordering; vector registers are stored fully byte-reversed (16 bytes) rather than per-lane swapped.

The FPU/VMX denormal conflict is handled with a compile-time enum class CSRState { Unknown, FPU, VMX } and a printSetFlushMode lambda that emits ctx.fpscr.enable/disableFlushMode() only on state change (with an 'Unconditional' variant out of Unknown), avoiding redundant rounding-mode writes.

UnleashedRecomp binds Xbox kernel imports to host C++ via GUEST_FUNCTION_HOOK(__imp__Name, HostFn) expanding to PPC_FUNC(__imp__Name){ HostToGuestFunction<HostFn>(ctx, base); }, with ArgTranslator marshalling integer args from r3..r10, float args from f1..f13, and returns into r3 (int/ptr) or f1 (float).

research.project: UnleashedRecomp (Sonic Unleashed Xbox 360 -> PC) + its toolchain XenonRecomp / XenonAnalyse / XenosRecomp
research.summary: UnleashedRecomp is the first shipped, fully-playable static recompilation of a complete AAA Xbox 360 (Xenon, PowerPC + VMX128) game to native PC. It is built on three tools by the same team: XenonAnalyse (static analysis: function boundary + jump-table recovery), XenonRecomp (PPC -> C++ lifter, one C++ function per guest function taking PPCContext& and a uint8_t* base), and XenosRecomp (Xenos shader microcode -> HLSL, then DXC -> DXIL/SPIR-V). The recompiled C++ links against a hand-written runtime that re-implements the Xbox 360 kernel/XAM/Direct3D/XAudio as host functions; the binding is done purely through the linker by defining strong symbols named __imp__<guest_name> that the lifter emitted as weak/extern. Crucially, the GPU layer does NOT emulate the raw Xenos command ring buffer — it hooks the guest's Direct3D 9-style device methods (SetRenderState, DrawPrimitive, etc.), enqueues them as RenderCommand structs to a lock-free render thread queue, and replays them on a custom cross-platform RHI called Plume (D3D12 + Vulkan 1.2). Both projects were 'guided by referencing Xenia' for the hardware-accurate semantics. The whole thing is heavily Clang-specific because the hooking/weak-linking and SIMDe vector lowering depend on Clang behavior.

dimensions.howItWorks: XenonAnalyse uses two strategies. (1) Functions that allocate a stack frame have explicit boundaries in the XEX .pdata segment (IMAGE_CE_RUNTIME_FUNCTION descriptors) and are read directly. (2) For the rest, it scans for branch-link (bl) targets to find function starts, then determines length by static walk of the code. Additional functions come from hardcoded helper-stub addresses (register save/restore thunks) and from manually supplied address/size pairs in the TOML. All discovered functions become entries in image.symbols, named sub_{:X} by hex address (fmt::format), and pushed into a `functions` vector used to resolve direct calls.
techniques: XEX .pdata IMAGE_CE_RUNTIME_FUNCTION parsing for exact frame-having boundaries
bl-target scanning for prologue-less / non-.opd functions
manual function list in TOML: functions = [{ address=0x..., size=0x... }]
named save/restore helper thunks supplied by address (restgprlr_14_address, savefpr_14_address, restvmx_64_address, etc.)
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: This directly attacks ps3recomp's 72% recall gap. PS3 ELF/PRX has .opd (function descriptors: entry+TOC) analogous to .pdata; functions NOT in .opd are exactly the ~1000 Ghidra finds. The transferable mechanism is the layered fallback: (.opd descriptors) + (bl/call-target scan) + (a manual TOML/JSON override list to bolt on the addresses Ghidra found but the heuristics missed). Critically, XenonRecomp does not try to be 100% automatic — it ships an escape hatch (config-supplied function and size) so a human can patch in the misses, which is exactly what an un-booted project needs to make progress.

dimensions.dimension: Indirect branches / jump tables / virtual calls
dimensions.howItWorks: Jump tables are detected by a pattern heuristic: find `mtctr r0` which is 'almost always followed by bctr'; XenonAnalyse emits the resolved table to a TOML file (switch_table_file_path, e.g. SWA_switch_tables.toml) listing the controlling register and the label targets. At codegen, a `bctr` with an associated switch table becomes a real C++ `switch (rN.u64){ case i: goto loc_XXXX; ... default: __builtin_unreachable(); }`. A `bctr/bctrl` with NO table becomes a fully dynamic call: PPC_CALL_INDIRECT_FUNC(rN.u32). Indirect/virtual calls are resolved at runtime via a 'perfect hash table' placed in memory just past the valid XEX region: dereferencing a 64-bit pointer at (original_instruction_address * 2) yields the host address of the recompiled function.
techniques: mtctr-then-bctr pattern recognition for switch tables
offline jump-table TOML consumed by the lifter -> native C++ switch + goto labels
perfect-hash function pointer table indexed by guest_addr*2, placed beyond XEX memory
PPC_CALL_INDIRECT_FUNC fallback for unresolved indirect targets
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: PS3 function pointers, vtables, and SPU branch-indirect (bi/bisl) are ps3recomp's named hard problem. Two transferable ideas: (1) the static mtctr+bctr table heuristic maps to PPC bctr on the PPU identically (same ISA), and the offline-TOML approach lets you escape the 'looks like a tail call' ambiguity by precomputing tables out-of-band. (2) The runtime perfect-hash table keyed on guest address is the general escape valve: ANY guest function pointer (vtable slot, callback) can be dispatched by looking up guest_addr -> host_fn at runtime, so you do not need to statically resolve every indirect edge — you only need every reachable function to be in the table. ps3recomp can build the same guest_addr->host_fn map and emit an indirect-dispatch helper.

dimensions.howItWorks: One C++ function per guest function with signature taking PPCContext& ctx and uint8_t* base (the 32-bit guest pointer base). Recompile() disassembles 4 bytes at a time (ppc::Disassemble) and emits C++ via a giant switch on insn.opcode->id. Register access goes through lambdas r(), f(), v() that decide per config whether a register is a local C++ variable or a field of ctx. Loads/stores use macros (PPC_LOAD_U64, PPC_STORE_U32) that byte-swap on access and are marked volatile; an MMIO variant PPC_MM_STORE_U32 exists but MMIO is largely unimplemented. bl to a known symbol emits a direct C++ call `name(ctx, base);` and sets ctx.lr unless skip_lr. Output is deliberately NOT decompiled/readable — it is a literal transliteration.
techniques: per-guest-function C++ emission, PPCContext& + base pointer ABI
opcode-id switch dispatch over disassembled instructions
r()/f()/v() accessor lambdas that promote registers to locals when ABI-safe
volatile byte-swapping load/store macros at every memory boundary
ctx.lr written before each call unless skip_lr optimization is on
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: ps3recomp already mirrors this (one C function per guest fn, ppu_context*, g_base+addr, BE swap at boundaries) — so XenonRecomp validates the architecture choice. The PPU is the SAME PowerPC ISA family, so the opcode-switch lifter and the load/store byte-swap macros are nearly 1:1 reusable; the main delta is 64-bit pointers (PS3 PPU is 64-bit) vs Xenon's 32-bit base trick. The 'volatile + reverse whole 16-byte vector' approach (see SIMD) is directly applicable. Lesson: keep output non-decompiled/transliterated — readability is not the goal, correctness and compile-throughput are.

dimensions.howItWorks: Most VMX (VMX128) instructions are lowered to x86 intrinsics (e.g. simde_mm_add_ps, simde_mm_add_epi8); ARM64 support comes free via the SIMDe (SIMD Everywhere) header library that maps the same intrinsic names onto NEON. For endianness, vector registers are NOT element-swapped — the recompiler reverses the ENTIRE 16-byte vector once. A subtle correctness fix: x86 VMX-equivalent ops flush denormals but the PPC FPU must preserve denormals, so the current FP control state is stored in the PPCContext and denormal-flushing is toggled on/off around vector vs scalar FP code.
techniques: VMX -> SIMDe intrinsics (one source, x86 SSE/AVX + ARM64 NEON targets)
whole-16-byte vector reversal instead of per-element swap for BE->LE
FP denormal-mode toggling tracked in the CPU context struct to reconcile FPU vs VMX denormal behavior
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: PS3 PPU has VMX/AltiVec (the same VMX the Xenon uses, minus the 128 extensions) and the SPUs have a custom 128-bit SIMD ISA. The SIMDe approach is directly transferable: lower PPU VMX and SPU vector ops to SIMDe intrinsics to get x86+ARM64 for free. The whole-vector-reversal trick solves the perennial BE vector layout problem cheaply. The denormal-mode insight is a real, non-obvious bug source ps3recomp will hit: Cell PPU/SPU and x86 disagree on denormal flushing, and tracking FP state in the context to toggle it is the fix. SPU ISA has no x86 1:1 mapping for some ops, so 'adaptable' not 'direct' for SPU.

dimensions.dimension: Kernel/HLE imports + NID-equivalent resolution (THE key lesson)
dimensions.howItWorks: This is the cleanest transferable mechanism. XenonRecomp emits, for every imported guest function, a weakly-linked C++ function plus a strong implementation symbol named __imp__<guest_name> (pattern: PPC_FUNC_IMPL(__imp__sub_X); PPC_FUNC(sub_X){ __imp__sub_X(ctx, base); }). The runtime then simply DEFINES the strong __imp__ symbols. Binding is done entirely by the LINKER — no runtime dispatch table needed. The runtime registers a host C++ function for a guest import with one macro: GUEST_FUNCTION_HOOK(__imp__KeSetEvent, KeSetEvent). Arguments are marshalled by a template machine (HostToGuestFunction / _translate_args_to_host): integers/pointers read from r3..r10 (pointers offset by base; >8 args spill to stack at 0x54), floats from f1..f13 via a separate FP ordinal; return value written to r3 or f1. Unimplemented imports are handled three ways: GUEST_FUNCTION_STUB(name) -> empty body; a logging stub LOG_UTILITY("!!! STUB !!!"); minimal-return stubs (return 0); or __builtin_debugtrap() for must-not-happen paths. imports.cpp has 200+ GUEST_FUNCTION_HOOK lines covering threads, sync primitives, memory, config.
techniques: weak PPC_FUNC alias + strong __imp__<name> implementation, resolved by the linker (no per-call lookup cost)
GUEST_FUNCTION_HOOK(guest_symbol, host_fn) one-line registration
template arg-marshalling: r3..r10 ints/ptrs, f1..f13 floats, stack spill at 0x54, ret in r3/f1
graceful-degradation tiers: STUB (empty) / logging stub / return-0 / debugtrap
incremental import coverage: implement only what the title actually calls
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: This is the single biggest lesson for ps3recomp's HLE/NID layer. ps3recomp resolves HLE via NID = SHA1(name)[:4] and a runtime table. The XenonRecomp insight is to make the lifter emit a STABLE symbol per import (e.g. __imp__<NID_or_name>) declared weak, and let the linker bind host implementations — replacing per-call NID-table lookups with zero-cost linker resolution. Provide a GUEST_FUNCTION_HOOK-style macro and a template marshaller mapping PPU ABI (r3-r10 / f1-f13, stack spill, TOC) to native C++ signatures so each LV2 syscall / cellXxx import is one line. Adopt the same degradation tiers so unimplemented NIDs link as logging stubs (return 0) instead of breaking the build — this lets the project BOOT with partial coverage, which is exactly ps3recomp's blocker. The template marshaller also auto-handles the BE swap of arguments/pointers.

dimensions.howItWorks: Memory is one giant linear reservation: struct Memory{ uint8_t* base; }; Translate(offset)=base+offset, MapVirtual(host)=(uint32_t)(host-base), IsInMemoryRange checks [base, base+PPC_MEMORY_SIZE). Guest 32-bit pointers index directly into this. Threads: each guest thread gets a GuestThreadContext that allocates one contiguous block (PCR 0xAB0 + TLS 0x100 + TEB 0x2E0 + STACK 0x40000) from a user heap; ctx.r1 = stack base, ctx.r13 = thread block (TLS), stored per-thread. ExCreateThread maps to a host std::thread (or pthread); the host thread blocks on a suspended flag then calls GuestThread::Start. setjmp/longjmp are redirected to native versions (config longjmp_address/setjmp_address) because Xenon has too many vector regs to save normally — the PPCContext even carries x86 CPU state for this.
techniques: single contiguous base reservation, pointer = base + guest32
MapVirtual/Translate inline host<->guest pointer conversion
per-thread guest stack+TLS+TEB+PCR in one heap allocation, r1/r13 set up manually
guest thread == host std::thread/pthread, suspend/resume via atomic flag wait
native setjmp/longjmp redirection, x86 state embedded in PPCContext
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: ps3recomp already uses host_ptr = g_base + guest_addr, so the Memory/Translate model matches and validates it. Transferable specifics: (1) lay out guest thread stack + TLS + a fake TEB/PCR analog in one allocation and set r1/r13 (PS3 PPU uses r1 stack, r13 small-data/TLS, r2 TOC) — ps3recomp needs the same for sys_ppu_thread_create. (2) Map LV2 thread syscalls to host std::thread with the same suspend/resume pattern. (3) The setjmp/longjmp redirection is needed on PS3 too (sys exceptions / C++ EH). For SPU, each SPU needs its own 256KB local-store buffer (analogous to the per-thread block) plus channel/mailbox state in its spu_context.

dimensions.dimension: GPU abstraction (Plume RHI, D3D12/Vulkan) and command capture
dimensions.howItWorks: Key architectural choice: UnleashedRecomp does NOT parse the raw Xenos PM4 command ring buffer. Sonic Unleashed calls a Direct3D 9-style API; the runtime HOOKS those guest device methods directly via GUEST_FUNCTION_HOOK (SetRenderState — templated per render-state type, SetTexture, SetSamplerState, SetVertexShader/SetPixelShader, SetVertexDeclaration, SetStreamSource, DrawPrimitive/DrawIndexedPrimitive/DrawPrimitiveUP, SetIndices, Clear, lock/unlock). Each hook pushes a RenderCommand struct onto a lock-free moodycamel::BlockingConcurrentQueue<RenderCommand> g_renderQueue, decoupling the guest thread from a dedicated render thread. The render thread dequeues and calls Proc* handlers (ProcSetRenderState, ProcDrawImGui, ProcUnlockTextureRect uploading via copy queues, ProcDestructResource) that drive Plume — a custom cross-platform RHI (RenderInterface/RenderDevice/RenderCommandQueue/RenderCommandList/PipelineState) over D3D12 and Vulkan 1.2, using bindless textures, shader specialization, flip-model present and waitable swapchains. Backend chosen at runtime in Video::CreateHostDevice (UNLEASHED_RECOMP_D3D12 flag).
techniques: hook high-level guest D3D9 device methods instead of parsing the GPU ring buffer
lock-free producer/consumer RenderCommand queue (moodycamel) -> dedicated render thread
custom RHI 'Plume' over D3D12 + Vulkan 1.2; bindless + specialization constants
copy-queue async texture uploads; flip-model + waitable swapchain for low latency
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: This is the most important strategic divergence for ps3recomp's RSX path. PS3 talks to RSX via cellGcmSys, which writes a raw NV40/NV47 FIFO/command buffer — there is no high-level D3D-style API to hook. So ps3recomp CANNOT use the 'hook the device methods' shortcut and is forced into the ring-buffer-parsing approach it already plans. BUT the transferable parts are: (1) the lock-free RenderCommand queue + dedicated render thread decoupling is directly reusable — parse the FIFO on one thread, replay translated commands on a render thread. (2) Plume itself is a ready-made, battle-tested cross-platform RHI over D3D12+Vulkan that ps3recomp could literally reuse as its backend instead of writing one. (3) If any PS3 title uses a higher-level wrapper (e.g. PSGL/libgcm helpers) those entry points could be hooked the UnleashedRecomp way to skip FIFO parsing for parts of the workload.

dimensions.howItWorks: XenosRecomp parses the Xbox 360 shader container (constant-buffer reflection, definitions, interpolators, vertex declarations, microcode instructions) — reflection data is MANDATORY or it won't run. It emits HLSL, compiled offline by DXC to DXIL (D3D12) and SPIR-V (Vulkan). At runtime guest shaders are matched to their recompiled versions by a 64-bit XXH3 hash lookup (works even for shaders embedded in the executable / uncompressed archives). Fixed constant layout: VS 4096B (256 float4), PS 3584B (224 float4) + shared; bool constants packed 16-into-a-32-bit-int. In Vulkan, constant-buffer GPU virtual addresses are passed as PUSH CONSTANTS and read via vk::RawBufferLoad through preprocessor macros. Vertex declarations become native D3D12/Vulkan input layouts; vertex data is endian-swapped before upload by treating buffers as uint32 arrays; unusual packed formats are unpacked in-shader via specialization constants (e.g. NORMAL/TANGENT/BINORMAL). Cube fetches use a local direction array indexed per cube instruction. 'Nearly every aspect was guided by referencing Xenia's shader translator.'
techniques: offline microcode->HLSL->DXC->DXIL/SPIR-V; runtime XXH3 hash maps guest shader bytes -> recompiled binary
mandatory reflection-driven constant buffer layout, bool constants bit-packed
Vulkan push-constant pointers + vk::RawBufferLoad for constant access
vertex declaration -> native input layout; uint32-array endian swap of vertex data; specialization-constant format unpacking
SPIR-V smol-v + zstd compression of the shader cache
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: RSX vertex/fragment programs are NV40 microcode (different ISA from Xenos), so the parser is not reusable, but the PIPELINE is: lift RSX shader microcode -> HLSL/GLSL -> compile to DXIL/SPIR-V offline, and at runtime map the guest shader program bytes to the recompiled binary by a content hash (XXH3) — RSX shaders are uploaded from guest memory just like Xenos, so the hash-lookup mapping is directly transferable. The endian-swap-vertex-data-as-uint32 trick and specialization-constant format unpacking are reusable for RSX vertex attributes. And the explicit dependency on Xenia for semantics maps to RPCS3's RSX implementation as ps3recomp's reference oracle.

dimensions.howItWorks: The guest XAudio driver-client API is hooked: XAudioRegisterRenderDriverClient, XAudioUnregisterRenderDriverClient, XAudioSubmitRenderDriverFrame. On register, the guest callback function pointer is resolved (g_memory.FindFunction) and stored; submitted frames go to XAudioSubmitFrame(samples). Samples are channel/sample reordered and endian-swapped (ByteSwap) from the guest's interleaved big-endian format before being handed to the host audio backend. There is even a debug raw-PCM dump path. XMA hardware-codec decode is via MMIO in the original — and that path is largely the unimplemented/unfinished MMIO mentioned in XenonRecomp; Unleashed sidesteps heavy reliance on it for the shipped title.
techniques: hook XAudio render-driver-client entry points; store guest callback pointer
periodic guest callback invocation to pull/submit audio frames
BE->LE sample byte-swap + channel reorder before host submission
raw PCM dump hook for debugging
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: PS3 audio is cellAudio (PCM mixing, analogous to XAudio — hook the libaudio entry points, store the port/callback, byte-swap BE float samples, submit to host SDL/XAudio2/WASAPI). The harder PS3 case is cellVdec/cellAdec (H.264/ATRAC3 media decode), which ps3recomp flags as incomplete and needing FFmpeg — UnleashedRecomp's experience confirms the strategy: do NOT emulate the hardware codec MMIO path; instead hook the high-level decode API and decode with a host library (FFmpeg for cellVdec/cellAdec ATRAC/AAC/H.264), submitting PCM/frames back through the same byte-swap+callback pattern.

dimensions.howItWorks: Two complementary mechanisms. (1) Function-level replacement via the weak-linking trick: define PPC_FUNC(sub_X) yourself to completely override a recompiled function while still being able to call __imp__sub_X (the original). This is how whole behaviors (renderer fixes, timing) are replaced. (2) Mid-asm hooks: in TOML, [[midasm_hook]] with name, address, registers=[...], and control options (return, return_on_true/false, jump_address[_on_true/false], after_instruction). The lifter injects, at that exact instruction address, a call to an extern C++ function (declared extern bool/void by name) receiving the named registers; the return value can force an early return or a jump to another guest address. Patches live in the patches/ dir, are config-gated (user-toggleable, not hardcoded), and cover delta-time/high-FPS fixes, aspect-ratio/UI, achievements, DOF (the DOF formula was reverse-engineered), reverse-Z, loading screens, etc. Mods use Hedge Mod Manager (Generations mod format).
techniques: weak PPC_FUNC override + __imp__ access to original (function-level monkeypatch)
TOML [[midasm_hook]] -> inject extern C++ call at any instruction, with register capture and conditional return/jump
before/after-instruction placement (after_instruction flag)
config-gated patches in a patches/ directory; reverse-engineered shader formulas (DOF, reverse-Z)
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: Both mechanisms transfer cleanly because ps3recomp uses the same one-C-function-per-guest-fn model. (1) Implement the weak/__imp__ override so individual PPU/SPU functions can be replaced in C++ — essential for HLE-ing functions that are too slow or wrong to recompile, and for game-specific fixes. (2) Add a TOML/JSON midasm-hook config so the lifter can inject host calls at arbitrary guest instruction addresses with register capture and conditional return/jump — invaluable for patching out indirect branches the analyzer can't resolve, stubbing problematic loops, or fixing timing without re-running analysis. This also gives a clean modding story later.

dimensions.howItWorks: Everything is driven by a single TOML config: [main] (file_path xex, patch_file_path xexp, out_directory_path, switch_table_file_path), [optimizations] (skip_lr, skip_msr, ctr_as_local, xer_as_local, cr_as_local, reserved_as_local, non_argument_as_local, non_volatile_as_local), explicit addresses for the register save/restore thunks and setjmp/longjmp, a functions list for manual boundaries, invalid_instructions list (e.g. {data=0x00000000,size=4}) to skip padding/EH data, and [[midasm_hook]] blocks. The local-variable optimizations (promoting CR/XER/CTR/regs to C++ locals) are the biggest perf win — they let the compiler delete the save/restore-thunk calls entirely; they assume strict ABI compliance. The toolchain is Clang 18+ / CMake 3.20+ only — non-Clang compilers are unsupported because the hooking/weak-linking and codegen rely on Clang behavior. Output is split across many translation units for parallel compilation.
techniques: single declarative TOML config controlling boundaries, optimizations, hooks, skipped bytes
register-to-local-variable optimizations contingent on ABI stability (huge size/perf win)
invalid_instructions allowlist to skip padding and exception-handling data
Clang-mandated toolchain; many TUs for parallel compile
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: ps3recomp should adopt a single declarative project config (TOML/JSON) that captures: manual function boundaries (the Ghidra-found misses), per-title save/restore-thunk addresses, jump-table file path, invalid/skip byte ranges, and midasm hooks. The ABI-driven 'promote registers to locals' optimization is directly portable to the PPU lifter (same ABI concept) and is where most of the runtime speed comes from. Consider standardizing on Clang for the same weak-linking/codegen guarantees, and split generated C per-function/per-module across TUs so the (huge, ~thousands of functions) output compiles in parallel.

standoutInnovations: Linker-resolved HLE binding: the lifter emits weak PPC_FUNC stubs aliased to strong __imp__<name> symbols, so providing a host implementation is just defining that symbol — no per-call NID/import dispatch table, zero runtime cost, and unimplemented imports degrade to logging/return-0 stubs so the project still LINKS and BOOTS with partial coverage. (Replaces ps3recomp's runtime NID table with linker resolution.)

Skip the GPU command ring buffer entirely by hooking the guest's high-level Direct3D 9 device methods and replaying them onto a custom cross-platform RHI (Plume) over D3D12+Vulkan, decoupled via a lock-free moodycamel command queue to a dedicated render thread.

Runtime guest-function-pointer dispatch via a 'perfect hash table' placed past the XEX memory region, indexed by original_instruction_address*2 — lets indirect/virtual calls work without statically resolving every edge (you only need every function present in the table).

Offline shader recompilation with runtime XXH3 content-hash lookup: guest shader bytes are hashed to find the pre-built DXIL/SPIR-V, robust even for shaders embedded in the executable; SPIR-V cache shrunk with smol-v + zstd.

Whole-16-byte vector reversal (not per-element swap) for big-endian VMX, plus tracking FP denormal mode in the CPU context to reconcile the PPC-FPU-preserves vs x86/VMX-flushes denormal mismatch — a real correctness bug class.

Register-to-C++-local optimizations (cr_as_local, ctr_as_local, non_volatile_as_local, ...) that let the compiler delete the GPR/FPR/VMX save-restore thunk calls entirely, the single largest perf/size win, gated on ABI compliance.

TOML-driven mid-asm hooks: inject an extern C++ call at ANY guest instruction address with selected registers and conditional return/jump — used both for game fixes and to paper over instructions/branches the static analyzer can't handle.

Both CPU and shader recompilers were explicitly built by referencing the Xenia emulator for hardware-accurate semantics — i.e. an existing accurate emulator is the semantic oracle for a recompiler (analog: RPCS3 for ps3recomp).
verifiableClaims: XenonAnalyse detects jump tables primarily by recognizing the `mtctr r0` instruction followed by `bctr`, and emits the resolved tables to a separate TOML file (e.g. SWA_switch_tables.toml) that XenonRecomp consumes to generate native C++ switch/goto.

Imports/functions are hooked via Clang weak-linking: XenonRecomp generates `PPC_FUNC_IMPL(__imp__sub_X)` plus a weak `PPC_FUNC(sub_X){ __imp__sub_X(ctx, base); }`, and the runtime registers host implementations with `GUEST_FUNCTION_HOOK(__imp__Name, HostFn)`; unimplemented imports use `GUEST_FUNCTION_STUB` or logging/return-0 stubs.

UnleashedRecomp does NOT parse the raw Xenos PM4/ring command buffer; it hooks guest Direct3D9-style device methods (SetRenderState, DrawPrimitive, SetTexture, etc.) and enqueues RenderCommand structs onto a moodycamel::BlockingConcurrentQueue processed by a dedicated render thread, replayed on the 'Plume' RHI over D3D12 and Vulkan 1.2.

XenosRecomp maps guest shaders to recompiled HLSL-derived DXIL/SPIR-V at runtime via a 64-bit XXH3 hash of the shader bytes, requires embedded reflection data, uses fixed constant-buffer sizes (VS 4096B/256 float4, PS 3584B/224 float4), and in Vulkan passes constant-buffer GPU addresses as push constants read with vk::RawBufferLoad.

XenonRecomp lowers VMX instructions to SIMDe intrinsics (x86 + ARM64 NEON), reverses entire 16-byte vectors for endianness rather than per-element, and tracks FP denormal mode in the PPCContext to reconcile PPC-FPU vs VMX denormal-flushing behavior; the toolchain requires Clang 18+ and CMake 3.20+.

research.project: PS2Recomp (ran-j) and PS2 EE/VU static recompilation — analyzed against ps3recomp's PPU/SPU/RSX/HLE pipeline
research.summary: PS2Recomp is an AOT static recompiler that turns PS2 ELF binaries into literal C++ (one C++ function per guest function, register state held in an R5900Context struct), structured as three tools mirroring ps3recomp: ps2xAnalyzer (Ghidra/native function discovery -> TOML), ps2xRecomp (Rabbitizer-based R5900 decode -> C++ codegen), and ps2xRuntime (mapped memory, syscall dispatch, hardware stubs). Its most transferable insight for the SPU problem is a clear split: it statically recompiles only the EE-stream vector code — the 128-bit MMI integer SIMD and VU0 *macro mode* (COP2) — by mapping each instruction directly onto host SSE intrinsics (PADDW -> _mm_add_epi32, VADD -> _mm_add_ps), exactly as XenonRecomp maps PPC VMX128. But it explicitly does NOT statically handle VU1 microprograms, because on PS2 those are separate microcode programs DMA-uploaded at runtime via VIF1/MPG into a private 16KB instruction memory (MicroMem1) and launched with MSCAL/CMSAR — the precise architectural analog of SPU code DMA'd into 256KB local store and started via the MFC. The two reference solutions to that exact problem are: (a) PCSX2's microVU, which JITs VU microprograms at runtime and keys/caches them by memcmp of the actual VU instruction-memory bytes against compiled ranges (so a VIF re-upload that changes the program triggers recompile); and (b) N64Recomp, which CAN statically recompile RSP co-processor microcode precisely because that microcode ships inside the ROM and is statically identifiable — the opposite of dynamically-uploaded VU1/SPU code. The strongest prior art for ps3recomp's PPU lifter remains XenonRecomp/UnleashedRecomp (also PowerPC + VMX, big-endian), which contributes concrete mechanisms for indirect branches (jump-table TOML + a runtime perfect-hash from original-instruction-address to recompiled function), function-boundary recovery (.pdata + branch-link scan + TOML overrides), register-as-local optimizations, and mid-asm hooks.

dimensions.dimension: VU microprograms vs SPU dynamically-loaded code (the central question)
dimensions.howItWorks: On PS2, VU1 (and VU0 in micro mode) run separate microcode programs that are NOT in the EE instruction stream: a game DMA-transfers a microprogram from main RAM through VIF1 using the MPG VIFcode into VU1's private 16KB MicroMem1 (at 11008000h region), then starts it with the MSCAL/MSCALF VIFcode or by writing CMSAR1. The program in MicroMem can be overwritten at any time by a later MPG upload. Because of this, PS2Recomp's README and source explicitly state 'VU1 microcode is not complete' and the r5900_decoder does NOT parse VIF packet headers or VU micro-instruction (dual 64-bit upper/lower) words — it only decodes COP2 macro-mode VU0 ops that appear inline in the EE stream. This is the same reason ps3recomp can't statically find SPU programs: SPU code is DMA'd into 256KB local store at runtime and launched via MFC, so it isn't a fixed region of the boot ELF the static analyzer sees.
techniques: VIF1 MPG upload into MicroMem1
MSCAL/MSCALF/CMSAR1 program start
static recomp deliberately scoped to EE-stream (macro) code only
treating dynamically-uploaded co-processor code as out-of-scope for AOT
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: Direct confirmation that the SPU is genuinely the VU1 of the PS3 and that NO production static recompiler attacks dynamically-uploaded vector co-processor code purely at AOT time. The actionable pattern for ps3recomp: (1) statically recompile any SPU programs that ARE present and identifiable in the boot image / overlay files (the N64Recomp-RSP case), and (2) for SPU code copied into local store at runtime, fall back to a runtime JIT or interpreter keyed on the local-store contents — do NOT expect the static pass to find it. The project's own gap note ('SPU code is often dynamically loaded, hard to find statically') is exactly the VU1 situation and should be handled the same way PCSX2 handles VU1, not the way the PPU stream is handled.

dimensions.dimension: Content-keyed JIT cache for dynamically-loaded vector code (PCSX2 microVU)
dimensions.howItWorks: PCSX2's microVU recompiler is the canonical runtime solution to the VU1 problem. The microProgram struct stores a full copy of the VU microprogram bytes (u32 data[mProgSize], 'Holds a copy of the VU microProgram'). Programs are indexed by start PC (microProgramList* prog[mProgSize/2]) and a std::deque<microRange> records which PC ranges have already been recompiled. To decide whether a cached compiled program is still valid for the current MicroMem contents, mVUcmpProg()/mVUcmpPartial() memcmp the cached data against live VU memory — but only over the compiled ranges (mVUsetupRange), which avoids spuriously invalidating on unrelated bytes. Pipeline state (the VU's Q/P latency, MAC/clip flags, branch-delay state) is matched via microBlockManager::search using exact register-state compare or a quick64 checksum, so the same byte-program at the same PC can have multiple compiled blocks specialized to different incoming pipeline states.
techniques: store a copy of the program bytes + memcmp to detect overwrite (self-modifying-code invalidation)
key compiled blocks by (start PC + incoming pipeline/flag state)
compare only over already-compiled PC ranges, not the whole memory
quick64 checksum fast-path before full state compare
deque of recompiled ranges to track coverage incrementally
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: This is the template for an SPU runtime tier in ps3recomp. When a guest DMAs code into a 256KB local store and starts it, the runtime should hash/memcmp the local-store code region to look up a previously-compiled native function; on miss, JIT (or interpret) it and cache keyed by content hash, not by guest address (the same code can be loaded at different LS offsets, and the same LS offset can hold different code over time). The memcmp-over-compiled-ranges trick directly addresses SPU code being patched/relocated. ps3recomp could even reuse its own spu_lifter as the JIT body, invoked on a local-store blob instead of the boot ELF.

dimensions.dimension: Statically recompilable co-processor code when it ships in the image (N64Recomp RSP)
dimensions.howItWorks: N64Recomp can statically recompile RSP microcode to C using the same instruction-by-instruction lifting it uses for the main MIPS CPU — because standard RSP microcode is stored in the ROM and is statically identifiable, so the AOT pass can find and translate it (it notes RSP overlays are not yet handled, i.e. only fixed/identifiable microcode). It also handles relocatable overlays for the main CPU: instructions carrying relocation data (lui/addiu/loads/stores) are emitted with an extra macro, e.g. 'lui $24,0x80C0' -> 'ctx->r24 = S32(RELOC_HI16(1754,0x630) << 16);', where 1754 is a section index the runtime uses to relocate the immediate. Functions/overrides come from a TOML config (input/output paths, stub list, skip list, single-instruction patches, planned [[patches.func]]/[[patches.hook]]).
techniques: lift co-processor ISA with the same per-instruction emitter as the main CPU
RELOC_HI16/RELOC_LO16 macros so immediates are fixed up at load time for relocatable code
TOML-driven stub/skip/patch overlay
tail-call detection: j/b that are tail calls become real C function calls
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: Establishes the decision rule for SPU: if an SPU program is embedded in the boot ELF or an overlay file (some titles statically embed SPU images), recompile it statically with spu_lifter exactly like N64Recomp does RSP — you do NOT need a JIT for those. The RELOC_* mechanism is also directly useful for ps3recomp's PRX/relocatable-module problem: rather than baking absolute addresses, emit relocation macros so the runtime can place modules. The 'tail call -> C call' rule helps ps3recomp's known indirect-branch gap.

dimensions.dimension: Mapping 128-bit SIMD (MMI/VU0 macro) to host intrinsics
dimensions.howItWorks: PS2Recomp keeps register state in R5900Context where GPRs are '__m128i r[32]' (128-bit, used by MMI), VU0 floats are '__m128 vu0_vf[32]', VU0 integer regs are 'uint16_t vi[16]', plus '__m128 vu0_acc', scalar vu0_q/vu0_p/vu0_i floats, hi/lo and hi1/lo1 (uint64_t), pc, sa, and 21 COP0 registers. The codegen emits host SSE intrinsics directly via macros in ps2_runtime_macros.h: PS2_PADDW(a,b)=_mm_add_epi32, PS2_PSUBW=_mm_sub_epi32, PS2_PAND/POR/PXOR=_mm_and/or/xor_si128, and VU0 macro ops PS2_VADD=_mm_add_ps, PS2_VMUL=_mm_mul_ps, PS2_VDIV=_mm_div_ps. Where no clean SSE mapping exists (e.g. MADD HI/LO accumulation, QFSRV funnel shift), it falls back to scalar helpers (Ps2HiLoToU64, Ps2SignExt32ToU64). GPR_U32/GPR_VEC accessors special-case register 0 to zero. Decoding leans on the Rabbitizer disassembler library for instruction descriptors (isBranch/isJump/isCall/hasDelaySlot/isReturn).
techniques: __m128i/__m128 fields in the context struct = host SIMD register-for-register
one macro per guest SIMD opcode -> one host intrinsic
scalar fallback for opcodes with no direct intrinsic
reuse Rabbitizer for instruction classification instead of hand-rolling tables
XYZW vector-field mask decoded from (raw>>21)&0xF for partial-register writes
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: ps3recomp's PPU VMX/AltiVec lifter should map vector ops directly to SSE/AVX (or SIMDe for ARM, per XenonRecomp) the same way, with the PPU context holding __m128 vmx[32]. For SPU's 128-bit ISA, the same register-for-register __m128i/__m128 modeling applies. The XYZW-field-mask handling is relevant because PS2 VU and PS3 SPU both do masked/partial vector writes that must be emitted as blends. The scalar-fallback pattern is the realistic answer for SPU/VMX opcodes (e.g. saturating, shuffle, fused-multiply-add quirks) that don't have a 1:1 host intrinsic.

dimensions.dimension: PPU prior art: VMX128, big-endian, register optimization (XenonRecomp/UnleashedRecomp)
dimensions.howItWorks: XenonRecomp is the closest analog to ps3recomp's PPU lifter: same PowerPC core + VMX SIMD, big-endian. It passes a context struct (all 32 GPRs, LR, CTR, XER, CR fields, VMX regs, FPU state, 32-bit base pointer) to every PPC function. Big-endian is handled by byte-swapping at every load/store and marking memory ops volatile to block unsafe reordering; for vectors it reverses the entire 16-byte quantity rather than per-element, so instructions must compensate (e.g. use WZY instead of XYZ in dot products). It models the FPU-vs-VMX denormal difference by storing FP mode in the context and toggling denormal-flush per instruction. Performance optimizations are TOML flags that promote hot guest registers to C locals (ctr_as_local, xer_as_local, cr_as_local, non_volatile_as_local, etc.), eliminating context loads/stores. Backends: x86 intrinsics or SIMDe for ARM64.
techniques: context struct passed to every function; selectively promote regs to locals via config
byte-swap + volatile at memory boundary for big-endian
reverse whole 16-byte vector once (not per element) and adjust lane indices in ops
per-instruction denormal-flush toggling to match VMX vs FPU semantics
recognize compiler-generated save/restore-GPR/FPR/VMX stubs by address (restgprlr_14_address etc.) and special-case them
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: Almost everything transfers 1:1 to the PPU lifter. ps3recomp already does big-endian conversion at memory boundaries; the volatile-marking and whole-vector-reversal lane-adjustment detail is a concrete correctness fix for VMX. The denormal-flush toggling matters for PPU FPU/VMX divergence. The save/restore-stub recognition is directly useful for ps3recomp's 72% function-detection recall: GCC/SN-generated register save/restore thunks are a recognizable pattern that can be matched by address/byte-pattern and stubbed instead of mis-detected.

dimensions.howItWorks: PS2Recomp's preferred path is a Ghidra script (ExportPS2Functions.java) that exports a function map as TOML+CSV; the native ps2xAnalyzer is the faster fallback but is 'less accurate on stripped retail games and more likely to miss internal callable entry points.' The recompiler then auto-discovers additional internal static entry targets and emits entry_... wrappers, and tries relocation-symbol auto-binding at call sites before falling back to raw address dispatch. XenonRecomp recovers boundaries from the XEX .pdata segment for functions with stack frames, scans for branch-link instructions for the rest, sizes them by static analysis, and lets the user supply explicit {address,size} pairs in TOML for the cases the analyzer mis-sizes (notably jump-table functions that look like tail calls). N64Recomp added a guard to error out when a detected function size is zero rather than silently emitting an empty body.
techniques: use a mature external disassembler (Ghidra) as the front-end and ingest its function list
auto-discover internal entry targets from call-target analysis and emit wrappers
prefer relocation/symbol binding at call sites over raw-address dispatch
manual {address,size} overrides in config for analyzer failures
fail-loud on zero-size detected functions
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: ps3recomp's exact gap is here (72% recall, ~1000 fns only Ghidra finds, reached by call-target analysis, not in .opd, no standard prologue). The transferable moves: (1) make Ghidra the authoritative front-end and ingest its function list as TOML (PS2Recomp already does this), (2) add an iterative call-target closure pass that promotes every discovered call/branch target to a function entry and emits a wrapper (PS2Recomp's entry_... mechanism), (3) the PS3 analog of .pdata is the .opd descriptor section plus the SN/GCC prologue — augment with branch-link/bl-target scanning for functions absent from .opd, exactly as XenonRecomp does for non-.pdata functions.

dimensions.dimension: Indirect branches / jump tables / virtual calls
dimensions.howItWorks: Three layered mechanisms across the projects. PS2Recomp emits indirect jr/jalr as a switch over known internal targets ('switch(jumpTarget){ case 0x..u: goto label_..; }') built from sortedInternalTargets, falling back to runtime->lookupFunction(addr). N64Recomp pattern-matches jr-with-jump-table into a C switch-case, and emits the generic indirect call as 'LOOKUP_FUNC(ctx->r25)(rdram, ctx);'. XenonRecomp's XenonAnalyse detects the canonical jump-table pattern (mtctr r0; bctr) and writes a switch_table TOML; virtual/function-pointer calls are resolved at runtime through a perfect hash table where dereferencing (original_instruction_address*2) yields the recompiled function address, with function regions exported as macros in ppc_config.h.
techniques: switch/goto over statically-known internal targets, runtime lookup as fallback
jump-table pattern recognition (mtctr+bctr / lw+jr) -> emit switch table to config
runtime perfect-hash map from original guest address to recompiled function pointer
mark every relocation/vtable target as a callable entry so the hash table is complete
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: ps3recomp lists indirect branches (fn pointers/vtables/switch tables) as a hard gap. The directly applicable answer is XenonRecomp's perfect-hash 'guest address -> native function' table: any computed call (PPU bctrl through a vtable, or an .opd function pointer) becomes a single hash lookup at runtime, which sidesteps needing to statically prove the target set. Combine with N64Recomp's static jump-table-to-switch recognition for the cases that ARE provable, and a TOML switch_table override for the cases that aren't. This also covers SPU branch-indirect once SPU code is being lifted.

dimensions.howItWorks: PS2Recomp maps guest RAM as a host buffer and resolves addresses with a hybrid fast/slow path: READ32(addr) checks PS2Runtime::isSpecialAddress(_addr) and routes MMIO/special regions to runtime->Load32, else takes FAST_READ32 which does Ps2FastRead32(rdram, addr & PS2_RAM_MASK) — a masked direct buffer index. Memory ops are wrapped in macros (READ32/WRITE32, GPR_U32/SET_GPR_U32) so the host representation can change without touching codegen. The runtime also does function registration and syscall dispatch and provides hardware stubs (GS/VU/file/system). This mirrors ps3recomp's host_ptr = g_base + guest_addr model.
techniques: host RAM buffer + address masking for the common case
isSpecialAddress() branch to route MMIO/registers to handler functions
all memory and register access behind macros for portability
central function registry + syscall dispatch table in the runtime
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: Validates ps3recomp's g_base+guest_addr design and adds the explicit fast/slow split: keep a hot inlined masked path for ordinary RAM and a predicate (isSpecialAddress) that diverts RSX GCM registers, SPU MMIO/mailbox/channel addresses, and LV2 syscall pages to handlers. For SPU specifically, channel reads/writes (mailbox, DMA list, decrementer) map naturally onto the isSpecialAddress -> handler pattern.

dimensions.howItWorks: PS2Recomp resolves OS/library calls by name through TOML 'stubs' (route a named function to an existing runtime handler) and 'skip' (emit a TODO_NAMED placeholder wrapper for intentionally-unimplemented functions). On stripped ELFs, stubs can be bound by address with handler@0xADDRESS syntax, and generic constant-return handlers exist (ret0@0xADDR, ret1@0xADDR, reta0@0xADDR) for trivially-stubbable calls. UnleashedRecomp implements a full 'Xbox 360 kernel translation layer' so original kernel/import calls are intercepted and reimplemented natively (analogous to LV2 + cell* libs), though the README doesn't detail the NID/import resolution mechanism.
techniques: name-based stub/skip lists in config
address-bound stubs (handler@0xADDR) for stripped binaries with no symbols
constant-return generic handlers (ret0/ret1/reta0) for cheap stubbing of unimportant calls
TODO_NAMED placeholders so unimplemented calls fail in an identifiable way
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: ps3recomp already resolves HLE via NID = SHA1(name)[:4]. The transferable additions: (1) the ret0/ret1/reta0 generic-handler idea is a fast way to neutralize the long tail of non-critical cell* calls so a title can boot before every lib is implemented; (2) the handler@0xADDR address-bound stub is the right tool when NID resolution fails or for raw syscall sites; (3) TODO_NAMED-style loud placeholders give a prioritized work-list of which imports actually get hit at boot — directly useful given ps3recomp has not booted a title end-to-end yet.

dimensions.dimension: Graphics: VU1->GIF->GS (PS2) vs RSX NV47 FIFO (PS3)
dimensions.howItWorks: PS2 graphics flow through three GIF PATHs into the GS: PATH1 = VU1 XGKICK (highest priority, direct VU1->GS), PATH2 = VIF1 DIRECT/DIRECTHL, PATH3 = GIF DMA channel 2 (16-quadword FIFO at 10006000h); only one PATH runs at a time, masked via GIF_MODE (10003010h), with GIF_STAT (10003020h) reporting FIFO occupancy. PS2Recomp stubs GS/VU/GIF and states 'Graphics Synthesizer and other hardware components need external implementation' — i.e. it punts the GPU entirely to an external HLE, just as ps3recomp routes RSX through cellGcmSys HLE into an NV47 FIFO parser. UnleashedRecomp instead recompiles the GPU side too: XenosRecomp translates Xenos shader microcode to HLSL, and a from-scratch renderer translates draw calls to D3D12 (SM6) or Vulkan 1.2 using bindless textures, shader specialization, and parallel transfer queues.
techniques: treat the GPU as an HLE boundary: parse the command FIFO, don't recompile the GPU
shader microcode -> HLSL transpile (XenosRecomp) as a separate recompiler
bindless textures + shader specialization + parallel transfer queues in the host backend
single-active-PATH arbitration / FIFO occupancy registers as the sync model
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: Confirms ps3recomp's RSX-as-HLE approach is the mainstream choice (PS2Recomp does the same with GS). The strongest concrete lesson is UnleashedRecomp's separate shader recompiler: ps3recomp will eventually need to transpile RSX fragment/vertex shader microcode (NV40-class) to HLSL/SPIR-V, and treating that as a sibling recompiler (a 'RsxShaderRecomp') rather than bolting it into the FIFO parser is the proven structure. The bindless + specialization renderer design maps onto the planned D3D12/Vulkan RSX backend.

dimensions.dimension: Tooling / config format (TOML overlay over a static binary)
dimensions.howItWorks: All three recompilers converge on a TOML config as the single hand-editable overlay that compensates for static-analysis limits. PS2Recomp keys: general.input, general.ghidra_output (CSV fn map), general.output, general.single_file_output, general.low_memory_mode, general.output_worker_threads, general.patch_syscalls/patch_cop0/patch_cache, general.stubs, general.skip, and [patches].instructions (raw per-address instruction replacement). XenonRecomp adds [main] file paths, switch_table_file_path, the register-as-local optimization flags, explicit functions=[{address,size}], invalid_instructions=[{data,size}] to skip exception-handler data, named save/restore-thunk addresses, longjmp/setjmp addresses, and [[midasm_hook]] entries (name, address, registers, return/jump-on-true/false, after_instruction). UnleashedRecomp uses XenonRecomp's PPC_FUNC/PPC_FUNC_IMPL weak-linking + __imp__ aliasing so a hand-written C++ function can override a recompiled one while still calling the original.
techniques: TOML as the authoritative overlay for everything static analysis can't infer
per-instruction patch table keyed by address
mid-asm hooks: inject a native callback at an arbitrary instruction with chosen registers and control-flow override
weak-linking + __imp__ alias so generated functions can be overridden/wrapped without editing generated code
config flags to skip data misread as code (invalid_instructions)
dimensions.relevanceToPS3: ps3recomp should adopt the same TOML overlay surface: function {address,size} overrides for its 72%-recall gap, a switch_table section and midasm_hook mechanism for indirect branches and runtime patches, and the PPC_FUNC/__imp__ weak-override pattern so HLE reimplementations, bug fixes, and mods can replace recompiled PPU/SPU functions without touching generated C. The per-instruction patch table is also how you neutralize cache/COP/syscall instructions that don't translate cleanly. invalid_instructions is directly relevant because PPC .opd/EH data and SPU local-store data get misread as code.

standoutInnovations: XenonRecomp's runtime perfect-hash table mapping (original_guest_instruction_address*2) -> recompiled-function pointer, which resolves vtable/function-pointer/indirect calls without statically proving the target set — the single most applicable fix for ps3recomp's indirect-branch and 72%-recall gaps.

PCSX2 microVU's content-keyed cache for dynamically-uploaded code: store a copy of the VU microprogram bytes and memcmp only the already-compiled PC ranges against live VU memory to detect VIF re-uploads, while keying compiled blocks by (start PC + incoming pipeline/flag state). This is the precise blueprint for an SPU runtime tier in ps3recomp.

The deliberate split between 'macro-mode vector code that lives in the main instruction stream' (statically recompiled to host SSE intrinsics) and 'micro/microcode that is DMA-uploaded into private memory at runtime' (left to a JIT/interpreter) — PS2 VU0-macro-vs-VU1 is the exact mirror of PS3 PPU-VMX-vs-SPU.

N64Recomp statically recompiling RSP microcode because it ships in the ROM: the rule that co-processor code IS statically recompilable when it's identifiable in the image, distinguishing the embedded-SPU-image case from the loaded-into-local-store case.

Register-for-register host SIMD modeling: holding 128-bit guest GPRs/vector regs as __m128i/__m128 fields in the context struct so MMI/VU0/VMX/SPU opcodes become single host intrinsics, with named scalar-fallback helpers only for opcodes lacking a 1:1 intrinsic.

XenonRecomp's whole-16-byte-vector reversal for big-endian (instead of per-element swap) plus per-instruction denormal-flush toggling to reconcile FPU-vs-VMX float semantics — concrete correctness mechanisms for the PPU VMX lifter.

Mid-asm hooks (inject a native callback at an arbitrary guest instruction with selected registers and control-flow override) as a general escape hatch for both bug-fixing recompiled code and enabling mods.
verifiableClaims: PS2Recomp's R5900Context stores general-purpose registers as '__m128i r[32]' and VU0 float registers as '__m128 vu0_vf[32]', and ps2_runtime_macros.h defines MMI/VU0 ops as direct SSE intrinsics (e.g. PS2_PADDW(a,b)=_mm_add_epi32, PS2_VADD(a,b)=_mm_add_ps).

PS2Recomp's README explicitly states 'VU1 microcode is not complete' and its r5900_decoder decodes only COP2 macro-mode VU0 instructions inline in the EE stream — it does not parse VIF packets or VU dual upper/lower micro-instructions.

PCSX2's microVU detects when a VU microprogram has been re-uploaded by storing a copy of the program bytes (microProgram.data) and comparing via mVUcmpProg/mVUcmpPartial (memcmp over the already-compiled microRange ranges), and caches compiled blocks keyed by start PC plus incoming pipeline state (microBlockManager::search, with a quick64 fast-path).

N64Recomp can statically recompile RSP microcode to C using the same per-instruction lifting as the main MIPS CPU (it only lacks support for RSP overlays), because standard RSP microcode ships in the ROM and is statically identifiable.

XenonRecomp resolves indirect/virtual calls at runtime via a perfect hash table where dereferencing (original instruction address * 2) yields the recompiled function address, and detects jump tables by recognizing the mtctr+bctr pattern, emitting a switch-table TOML.

research.project: Decompilation ports (Ship of Harkinian, sm64 decomp, splat/spimdisasm, asm-processor) vs static recompilation (N64Recomp/Zelda64Recomp, XenonRecomp/UnleashedRecomp) — and the decomp→recomp bridge
research.summary: There are two distinct retro-revival pipelines and they share a single load-bearing artifact: a symbol/boundary map. Matching decompilation (sm64, OoT/Ship of Harkinian) rewrites the binary as C that compiles byte-for-byte identical to the original; its toolchain is splat (Python binary splitter) + spimdisasm (MIPS disassembler with automatic function/pointer/jump-table detection) + asm-processor (lets unmatched functions stay as inline GLOBAL_ASM inside C while preserving byte layout). This is extremely high-effort but yields 100% function recall and full struct/symbol knowledge. Static recompilation (N64Recomp, XenonRecomp) instead mechanically lifts each guest function to one C/C++ function operating on a CPU-context struct, requiring far less per-game work but inheriting the binary's hard problems: function-boundary recall, indirect branches, and jump tables. The crucial finding for ps3recomp is that these are not rivals but a pipeline: N64Recomp consumes an ELF whose symbol table (function boundaries, data symbols, relocations) is produced by exactly the decomp toolchain (splat/spimdisasm), and Zelda64Recomp reuses decomp-derived headers/structs/function symbols for mods and enhancements. The recompilers' real innovations are in their config formats (TOML lists of manually-supplied function boundaries, switch tables, invalid-instruction ranges, register-save/restore stubs, mid-asm hooks) and runtime tricks (LOOKUP_FUNC for unresolved indirect calls, whole-16-byte vector reversal for big-endian SIMD, register-as-local optimization passes). XenonRecomp is the closest prior art to a PS3 PPU lifter because Xenon is also big-endian PowerPC with 128-bit VMX.

dimensions.howItWorks: Two opposite philosophies. DECOMP side: splat+spimdisasm do automatic function detection by scanning for jal/bl targets, branch-and-link return points, alignment, and prologue patterns, AND crucially let humans curate a symbol_addrs file (lines of the form `func_name = 0x80012345; // type:func size:0x40 rom:0x1234`) so any function the heuristics miss is supplied by hand — over a project's life this curated map converges to 100% recall. RECOMP side: N64Recomp does NOT detect functions itself; it requires an ELF whose symbol table already defines every function boundary/name (typically produced by the decomp/disasm setup), and falls back to a TOML `functions` list of explicit (address,size) pairs for anything missing. XenonAnalyse detects functions two ways: (1) the .pdata exception-directory segment gives exact boundaries for every function with stack allocation/unwind data, (2) for the rest it scans for branch-link instructions and statically computes length, with a TOML `functions` override for failures.
