code.currentApproach:
ps3recomp discovers PPU function boundaries with three overlapping, independently-maintained implementations, plus a separate SPU detector and an external Ghidra oracle that is only used for measurement/naming.

PPU primary detector — tools/find_functions.py::FunctionFinder (find_functions.py:137). Input is the full instruction stream produced by disassembling every executable PT_LOAD (flags&1) with ppu_disasm.disassemble_bytes (find_functions.py:635-639). exec_ranges are [p_vaddr, p_vaddr+p_filesz). It builds an addr->index dict (find_functions.py:149-151) and a dict[start_addr]->Function (start,end,stack_size,calls,callers,has_prologue/epilogue,is_leaf) (find_functions.py:99-126). run() executes five passes in order (find_functions.py:480-513):
 (1) find_prologue_functions: linear scan for `mflr r0` (find_functions.py:164), then within the next 5 insns requires `stw/std r0,X(r1)` and optionally `stwu/stdu r1,-Y(r1)`; extracts frame size from the stdu displacement (find_functions.py:174-188). Backs the start up one insn if the stack-alloc precedes the mflr (ELFv1 ordering) (find_functions.py:194-209). End = first `blr` (epilogue confirmed if a `mtlr r0` is within 3 insns before it), else the next `mflr`, else +100 insns (find_functions.py:217-244). Collects `bl` targets into func.calls.
 (2) find_leaf_functions: gathers `bl` targets from known funcs plus any `bl` whose source is inside an already-covered range (phantom filter, find_functions.py:270-275); for each uncovered target scans up to 200 insns to a `blr` (find_functions.py:286-306).
 (3) find_branch_target_functions: collects targets of `b`/`bc...` (excluding bl/blr/bctr/bctrl/blrl) whose SOURCE sits inside a covered function, then promotes uncovered targets, scanning <=500 insns to a blr/next-start (find_functions.py:327-387).
 (4) apply_seeds + drop_prologue_slivers (only if seeds present): registers every .opd/entry seed as a start bypassing min_size, each ending at its first blr bounded by the next start within a 2000-insn window (find_functions.py:398-429); then deletes heuristic starts that sit <=32 bytes after a seed with no intervening blr/b/rfid (mid-prologue anchors) (find_functions.py:431-459).
 (5) clip_overlaps: trims each end to the next start so bytes belong to <=1 function; inter-function gaps (padding/data) are intentionally left unattributed (find_functions.py:461-478). build_call_graph populates callers (find_functions.py:308-313).

.opd seeding — collect_opd_seeds (find_functions.py:519-587) does NOT trust section names; it scans every non-exec PT_LOAD data segment for {code,toc} u32 pairs where code is 4-aligned and in exec range and toc is a plausible data pointer (nonzero, not in text, within the bounding memsz span of non-exec segments, so BSS/gaps count) (find_functions.py:557-565); keeps TOC values that repeat >=16 times (find_functions.py:567), then collects every code paired with a kept TOC. ELF entry descriptor is resolved and added (find_functions.py:576-585). A warning fires if a >256KB text segment yields <=1 descriptor (find_functions.py:657-660). This shape-based scan is the fix described in broad-testing-findings.md:50-68 (flOw 31k->51.5k, Marvel UA 28k->51.4k).

PPU loader detector — tools/ppu_loader.py (a separate, simpler path) emits <name>.functions.json with {start,end,toc,opd}. It finds the OPD by the section that tightest-contains e_entry (ppu_loader.py:65-76), walks 8-byte {func,toc} descriptors sequentially until one stops looking valid (func not in code) (ppu_loader.py:79-96), picks module TOC as the most frequent toc, and sets end = next func start or segment hi (ppu_loader.py:180-190). It also parses ET_EXEC firmware imports via proc_prx_param(PT 0x60000002)->libstub (magic 0x1B434CEC), walking nid_tbl/stub_tbl (ppu_loader.py:115-147).

Legacy/fallback detector — ppu_disasm.py::detect_functions (ppu_disasm.py:1071-1118) is a minimal prologue+blr scanner with no .opd/leaf/branch/seed passes. ppu_lifter.py uses it as the fallback when --functions is not supplied (ppu_lifter.py:2289).

Lifter-side discovery (consumes the JSON, then adds more) — ppu_lifter.py reads func_bounds from --functions (ppu_lifter.py:2284-2290) and then runs: discover_jump_tables (ppu_lifter.py:2073-2158) which finds `mtctr;bctr` switch dispatchers, reads absolute or base-relative gcc offset tables from TOC, bounds case count via the cmplwi/cmpwi before the bctr (default 256 if absent, ppu_lifter.py:2140-2141), and promotes each in-text case target to a small standalone function (ppu_lifter.py:2322-2335); and generate_mid_function_entries (ppu_lifter.py:1802-1878) which, iterated up to 25 passes (ppu_lifter.py:2381-2387), turns referenced-but-undefined call/branch targets into tail-entry functions (target..containing-func end) or, for gap-resident targets, standalone funcs bounded by the next start. Indirect calls (bctr/bctrl and conditional *ctr) are emitted as runtime ps3_indirect_call(ctx) dispatch (ppu_lifter.py:744-773), i.e. resolved dynamically, not statically.

SPU detector — tools/find_spu_functions.py operates on an SPU ELF (extracted by extract_spu_images.py, which byte-scans the PPU image for 7F454C46/EI_DATA=2/e_machine=23 blobs, extract_spu_images.py:85-98). Seeds from e_entry, STT_FUNC symbols (using st_size for exact bounds when nonzero, find_spu_functions.py:234-238), and all resolved br/bra/brz/brnz/brsl/brasl targets (find_spu_functions.py:140-165). End discovery walks to `stop/stopd`, unconditional `br/bra/iret`, `bi $r0` (SPU ABI return), the next start, or code end (find_spu_functions.py:191-213), then coalesces overlaps. Emits {start,end} JSON and reports function coverage % of .text (data tail = .rodata in .text).

Ghidra path — ghidra_analyze.py runs analyzeHeadless with processor PowerPC:BE:64:64-32addr (ghidra_analyze.py:30) and the ExportAnalysisJson.java post-script, dumping functions/symbols/strings(/decompiled).json. ghidra_names.py turns these into a {addr:{label,cident,src}} map by priority: real symbol/Ghidra name, else a distinctive referenced string (C++ qualified > path basename > multi-token ident; stopword/ALL-CAPS filtered) (ghidra_names.py:62-118,194-214). The harness tier 6 (ps3_recomp_harness.py:362-406) only COMPARES Ghidra's function set to find_functions' starts to compute recall (~71.8% on Simpsons, broad-testing-findings.md:93-110). Ghidra's confirmed starts are NOT folded back as seeds; only names.json is consumed by the lifter as comments (ppu_lifter.py:2347-2361).
strengths: OPD-first seeding is the correct architectural choice for PPC64 ELFv1: collect_opd_seeds treats the .opd function-descriptor table as ground truth for every address-taken function, which is exactly what heuristic prologue scanning cannot recover. Seeds bypass min_size and are verified at the end (find_functions.py:677-684).

The .opd detector is robust to stripped binaries: it ignores section names entirely and locates the table by SHAPE (4-aligned in-exec code + repeated plausible TOC pointer, >=16-repeat threshold), and correctly relaxes the TOC test to include BSS/inter-segment gaps (TOC base ~= .got+0x8000). This fix more than doubled detection on flOw and Marvel UA (find_functions.py:551-567; broad-testing-findings.md:50-68).

Phantom-suppression is principled: leaf and branch passes only trust bl/branch instructions whose SOURCE already sits inside a detected function, because raw rodata embedded in .text decodes into spurious branches. Real code never branches into data, so source-filtering removes phantoms without losing real targets (find_functions.py:268-275, 341-358).

Conservative range model avoids garbage: clip_overlaps guarantees each byte belongs to <=1 function and deliberately leaves inter-function padding/data unattributed rather than sweeping it into a function (find_functions.py:461-478, 405-407).

Self-aware quality measurement: the harness runs Ghidra as an independent oracle and reports recall/extra with concrete missed addresses (ps3_recomp_harness.py:391-403), and find_functions warns loudly when a large text segment yields <=1 descriptor (find_functions.py:657-660). The project quantifies its own ~72% recall gap (broad-testing-findings.md:89-110).
SPU detector exploits symbol sizes when present for exact boundaries and seeds non-call branches too, preventing unresolved cross-function spu_func_X symbols (find_spu_functions.py:234-242, 146-165).

Lifter-side discovery genuinely recovers statically-invisible targets: gcc switch jump tables (absolute and base-relative offset form) are parsed from the TOC and promoted (ppu_lifter.py:2073-2158), and the iterated mid-function/gap-resident pass guarantees every referenced func_X is emitted, preventing dangling-symbol link failures (ppu_lifter.py:1802-1878).

gaps.gap: ~28% of functions are missed (recall ~71.8%): ~1,037 functions Ghidra finds are not detected. These are call-target-reachable but absent from .opd and lack a standard prologue, so no pass in find_functions promotes them. The lifter inherits the gap, and any indirect/static call into them lands on an unlifted address.

Ghidra's confirmed function starts are never folded back as seeds — the only documented remedy for the recall gap is explicitly listed as future work. Tier 6 computes the missed set (ps3_recomp_harness.py:396) but discards it; only names.json (comments) is consumed by the lifter (ppu_lifter.py:2347-2361). No recursive call-target/linear-sweep recovery exists to close the gap automatically.

Functions with multiple returns are truncated. Every pass ends a function at its FIRST blr (prologue pass find_functions.py:227-235, leaf find_functions.py:295-298, branch find_functions.py:374-379, seed find_functions.py:421-424). Any code after an early-return blr (common: guard clause `...; blr; <main body>`) is left unattributed unless separately reached as a branch/gap target. apply_seeds' own docstring concedes this and relies on the lifter's discovery to recover stragglers (find_functions.py:405-407).

Indirect branches (function pointers, vtables, computed switch) are not resolved statically at all — every bctr/bctrl becomes a runtime ps3_indirect_call(ctx). The detector cannot enumerate vtable/function-pointer targets, so an address-taken function only gets discovered if its .opd descriptor was found; if the .opd table is missed, the first indirect call crashes. Only gcc switch jump tables are statically recovered.
gaps.evidence: tools/ppu_lifter.py:744-773; docs/broad-testing-findings.md (known gaps: indirect branches); tools/find_functions.py:347 (bctr/bctrl explicitly excluded from branch-target pass)

gaps.gap: Three divergent OPD/boundary implementations can disagree and there is no single source of truth: shape-based collect_opd_seeds (find_functions.py:519), section-containing-entry parse_opd (ppu_loader.py:65-96), and the minimal prologue scanner ppu_disasm.detect_functions (ppu_disasm.py:1071). ppu_loader's section-based OPD location fails on stripped EBOOTs where section headers are absent (find_opd returns None,None) and its descriptor walk stops at the first invalid entry, unlike the frequency-thresholded scan.

The lifter's fallback detector is severely degraded: when --functions is omitted, ppu_lifter falls back to ppu_disasm.detect_functions, which has NO .opd seeding, no leaf/branch/seed passes, and requires a textbook prologue. This silently produces a tiny function set (the very failure mode broad-testing-findings.md warns about) with no warning.

~2,500 'extra' starts vs Ghidra are unaudited — a mix of genuine .opd address-taken functions Ghidra folded into callers and likely false positives, but the toolkit does not classify them, so an unknown fraction are spurious functions that get lifted as garbage.

Heuristic end-of-function fallbacks are arbitrary magic numbers with no validation: +100 insns when no blr is found in the prologue pass (find_functions.py:244), 200-insn leaf scan window (find_functions.py:288), 500-insn branch scan (find_functions.py:374), 2000-insn seed window (find_functions.py:417). A function exceeding any window gets a wrong end; clip_overlaps only fixes overlaps, not over-runs into gaps within the window.

SPU code that is dynamically loaded into local store (DMA'd at runtime, not present as a static embedded ELF) is undiscoverable: detection only sees SPU ELF blobs byte-scanned out of the PPU image. The project itself flags this as a known gap.
gaps.evidence: tools/extract_spu_images.py:85-98; docs/broad-testing-findings.md (known gaps: SPU dynamically loaded)

gaps.gap: Jump-table case count is guessed when the bound check is absent: discover_jump_tables defaults to reading 256 table entries when no preceding cmplwi/cmpwi is found (ppu_lifter.py:2140-2141), and the table-base is only resolved when loaded as lwz rX,disp(r2) directly off the TOC — register-indirect or multi-step base computations are not handled, so those switch dispatchers yield no case targets.

Absolute branch-and-link calls (bla, opcode 18 with AA=1, LK=1) are not collected as call targets. _is_bl matches only mnemonic=='bl' (find_functions.py:82), but ppu_disasm emits 'bla' for absolute calls (ppu_disasm.py:159-163); any function reached only via bla is missed by the leaf pass.

exec_ranges use p_filesz, not p_memsz, and the disassembler treats all of .text as code; embedded rodata/jump-tables inside the executable segment are disassembled as instructions and only filtered downstream by source-coverage heuristics, not by a data/code classification. There is no literal-pool or alignment-padding detection.

ppu_loader.parse_imports blindly trusts the libstub walk and reads u32s without bounds-checking the returned read_vaddr (e.g. read_vaddr(va,1)[0] will throw if the address is unmapped) and stops the whole import scan on the first zero-size stub entry, which can truncate valid import tables.

code.area: PPU disassembly and lifting to C
code.currentApproach:
The PPU path is a two-stage Python toolchain (tools/ppu_disasm.py -> tools/ppu_lifter.py) feeding a C/C++ runtime (runtime/ppu/*).

DISASSEMBLER (ppu_disasm.py): A single big if/elif decode() dispatches on the 6-bit major opcode (bits 0-5) and sub-opcode tables for X/XO/XL/MD/MDS/VX/VA forms. bits()/bit() use PowerPC MSB=0 numbering. Produces an Instruction(addr, raw, mnemonic, operands, comment) with operands as a formatted text string (e.g. "r3, 0x10(r4)", "v2, v3, v4"). Coverage is broad: integer arith/logical/shift, 32- and 64-bit rotates (rldicl/r/c/imi, rldcl/r), DS-form ld/std, indexed loads/stores, lwarx/stwcx., SPR (mfspr/mtspr decoded to mflr/mtlr/mfctr/mtctr), CR-logical, FP opcd 59/63, and a large hand-curated VMX/AltiVec table (opcd 4 + lvx/stvx under opcd 31). Comments in the file note prior XO-table bugs in the AltiVec range that were corrected against kakaroto/ps3ida and NXP ALTIVECPEM. Unknown encodings fall through to placeholder mnemonics like op31_x{xo}, vmx_x{xo}, rld??, or ".word 0x...". detect_functions() does naive prologue scanning (mflr r0 followed within 3 insns by std/stw r0,X(r1)) and ends a function at the next blr (or bctr if followed by mflr) — but the production path uses an external --functions JSON (find_functions.py / Ghidra) instead.

LIFTER (ppu_lifter.py): PPULifter._translate_op() is a ~1500-line if-ladder matching on the mnemonic STRING and parsing the operand string with regex (_reg_idx, _disp_base, _imm). Each guest function becomes one C function `void func_<ADDR>(ppu_context* ctx)`; instructions become inline C statements mutating ctx->gpr[]/fpr[]/vr[]/cr/lr/ctr/xer. Internal branches become `goto loc_<addr>;` with emitted labels; cross-function/cross-fragment branches set a TLS `g_trampoline_fn` and return (an iterative trampoline drain replaces deep host recursion); `bl` emits `func_<tgt>(ctx); DRAIN_TRAMPOLINE(ctx);`; `bctr`/`bctrl` emit `ps3_indirect_call(ctx)`; `sc` emits `lv2_syscall(ctx)`. Record (Rc=1) forms get a generic CR0-from-result append in _translate() (signed compare vs 0 + XER[SO]). Memory ops call vm_read*/vm_write* helpers; VMX ops are emitted as raw inline loops over pointer-cast lanes of ctx->vr[]. A jump-table discovery pass (discover_jump_tables) recognizes gcc `lwz rB,disp(r2); lwzx; add; mtctr; bctr` switch dispatchers (absolute and base-relative offset tables), reads the table out of the loaded image via TOC, and adds each case target as a small standalone function. A multi-pass generate_mid_function_entries() creates tail-entry wrappers for branch/call targets that land inside or between already-lifted functions (up to 25 passes). Lifting fans out to a multiprocessing Pool; output is split into ~600k-line .cpp chunks plus a header (ppu_recomp.h) that redefines ppu_context and a sentinel-terminated function_table[]. The lift can also consume a Ghidra name map (--names) emitted as comments.

RUNTIME: ppu_context.h is the canonical state struct (32 gpr/fpr/vr, cr/lr/ctr/xer/fpscr/vscr/cia, reservation fields) plus CR/XER helper inlines; vr[] is u128 (from ps3types.h, union with _u64/_u32/_u8/_s32/_f32). ppu_memory.h does host_ptr = vm_base + addr with ps3_bswap at every boundary and C11-atomic lwarx/stwcx./ldarx/stdcx.. ppu_loader.cpp is the actual runtime the lifted code links against: big-endian vm_read/write with optional OOB bounds-check, an open-addressing addr->fn hash registry, ps3_indirect_call dispatch (with a 2000-iteration stuck-loop abort), a big-endian ELF64 loader, OPD resolution, ppu_run entry, and lv2_syscall (only syscalls 352/330/403 implemented; everything else logs and returns gpr[3]=0 "CELL_OK"). ppu_hle.cpp resolves firmware imports by 32-bit NID through a flat table + a context-aware override table, marshaling gpr[3..10] into a generic uint64x8 adapter; unresolved NIDs return gpr[3]=0.
strengths: Broad, real-world instruction coverage. The disassembler and lifter together handle the integer/logical/shift core, both 32- and 64-bit rotate-mask families (rlwinm/rlwimi/rlwnm, rldicl/r/c/imi, rldcl/r) with correct mask helpers, DS-form and indexed loads/stores with update-form write-back, FP single/double arith + conversions, atomics, byte-reverse, and a large VMX/AltiVec subset (vperm, vsel, vsldoi, lvlx/lvrx, splats, packs, saturating arith, FP vector ops).

The trampoline + iterative-drain design (g_trampoline_fn / DRAIN_TRAMPOLINE) is a genuinely thoughtful solution to a hard recomp problem: converting cross-fragment fallthrough and backward branches into iteration instead of unbounded host recursion that would overflow the native stack.

Jump-table (computed bctr) discovery handles both absolute and gcc base-relative offset tables by reading the actual table data through the TOC, recovering switch-case targets that pure static branch analysis cannot see.

Multi-pass mid-function entry resolution closes the gap where branch/call targets land inside or between already-lifted functions, partitioning gaps at boundaries so adjacent entries do not swallow each other; gap-resident targets are promoted to their own functions to avoid referenced-but-undefined link errors.

Several non-obvious correctness fixes are present and documented in-code: full 64-bit add (not truncated, to keep SWAR strlen working), CTR masked to 32 bits on mtctr to avoid sign-extended infinite loops, dcbz implemented as a real 128-byte memset (not no-oped), conditional-return forms (beqlr/bnelr/...) emitted as real returns instead of no-op comments, and update-form base write-back.

Memory model is clean and consistent: a single vm_base + guest_addr translation with byte-swap localized to the runtime accessors, plus C11-atomic load-reserve/store-conditional and an OOB guard that degrades a stray access to a logged zero read instead of a host segfault, which is well-suited to incremental first-boot debugging.

Lifting is parallelized across processes with workers re-disassembling only their own byte ranges, and output is chunked at function boundaries to stay under the MSVC source-line limit and allow parallel/incremental compilation.

gaps.gap: ppu_ops.h (the entire PPU_ADD/PPU_LWZ/PPU_RLWINM... macro library) is dead parallel code: the lifter emits raw inline C and never references these macros (grep for PPU_ADD(/#include "ppu_ops in ppu_lifter.py returns nothing). The two implementations have already diverged in semantics (e.g. ppu_ops.h tracks XER[CA] in ADDIC/ADDC/SUBFC/SRAW/SRAWI and saturates SLW>=32 to 0; the lifter's emitted addic/addc/slw do not, or do so differently), so the macro file is a misleading source of truth.
gaps.evidence: runtime/ppu/ppu_ops.h:30-431 vs ppu_lifter.py:333-475 (no PPU_* macro is ever emitted)

gaps.gap: Combined decrement-and-condition branches (bdnzt/bdnzf/bdzt/bdzf and their lr/ctr variants) are not decoded into a composite condition. _branch_condition strips 'lr'/'ctr' then looks up the whole remaining mnemonic tail in cond_map; a name like 'dnzt' or 'dnzeq' is absent, so it hits the default '/* cond */ 1' (always true) — silently turning a CTR-counted conditional loop into an unconditional branch/return. Only plain dnz/dz are in the map.
gaps.evidence: ppu_lifter.py:1764-1796 (_branch_condition cond_map has only dnz/dz/eq/ne/lt/ge/gt/le/so/ns; default returns 1)

gaps.gap: _branch_condition tests CR bits with ((ctx->cr >> shift) & MASK) where shift=(7-field)*4 but does NOT mask the field to 4 bits first. For any field other than CR7, the >>shift leaves higher CR fields in the upper bits; &8/&4/&2/&1 happens to isolate the right bit only because those masks are within the low nibble — this is actually correct for the true tests, BUT the 'ge/le/ne/ns' forms use boolean NOT of the same expression, which is fine. The real latent issue: the masks assume bit positions LT=8,GT=4,EQ=2,SO=1 within the nibble, matching ppu_context CR layout, so it works — however the unconditional/unknown fallback returning literal 1 (default) is the dangerous path, shared with the bdnz combo gap above.

XER carry (CA) and overflow (OV/SO) are only partially and inconsistently modeled. The inline lifter implements CA for adde/addc/subfc/subfe/addze/addme/subfme/subfze, but plain add/addi/subf/neg and the o-form (addo./subfo. etc.) do NOT set OV/SO — the 'o' suffix is accepted by the decoder and the Rc CR0 path runs, but overflow is never computed. Code that branches on summary-overflow (so/ns) after an o-form will read stale XER[SO].
gaps.evidence: ppu_lifter.py:337-355 (add/subf/neg ignore OE/XER); decoder adds 'o' at ppu_disasm.py:503-512 but lifter never computes OV

gaps.gap: Record-form (Rc=1) CR0 update in the lifter computes a SIGNED-vs-zero comparison on the full 64-bit result for ALL dot-forms, including 32-bit operations (e.g. addic., and. on 32-bit values, slw./srw.). On a true PPU, CR0 for word operations reflects the 64-bit GPR after the defined sign/zero-extension, which the handlers do produce — but for ops whose handler leaves a non-canonical 64-bit value, CR0 sign can be wrong. Also stwcx./stdcx. are excluded (self-handled) but FP/VMX dot-forms are excluded by name prefix only (f/v/mt/mf), so a hypothetical non-prefixed dot-form would get an incorrect CR0.
gaps.evidence: ppu_lifter.py:295-308 (_translate generic CR0 append, _CR0_SELF_HANDLED only stwcx./stdcx.)

gaps.gap: lv2_syscall implements only 3 syscalls (352 memory size, 330 mmapper_allocate_address, 403 tty_write); every other syscall logs (first 30) and blindly sets gpr[3]=0 (CELL_OK). sys_mmapper_allocate_address returns a fabricated VA from a static bump allocator with no backing-memory mapping, so subsequent accesses to that VA hit the OOB guard / unmapped region.
gaps.evidence: runtime/ppu/ppu_loader.cpp:162-219 (default case: gpr[3]=0; comment 'Most syscalls are still stubbed ... return CELL_OK')

gaps.gap: HLE NID dispatch returns gpr[3]=0 for any unresolved import (logs first 40), and the generic adapter passes raw GPR values as both integer and pointer arguments with NO host<->guest address translation. Any cellXxx function taking or returning a guest pointer is wrong unless it has a hand-written ctx wrapper; the file's own comment acknowledges this.
gaps.evidence: runtime/ppu/ppu_hle.cpp:57-73 (generic uint64x8 adapter, no translation; unresolved -> gpr[3]=0)

gaps.gap: Indirect-branch / function-pointer resolution is fundamentally a runtime lookup that fails open. ps3_indirect_call hashes CTR and, if unregistered, returns without doing anything (after a stuck-loop abort at 2000 repeats). Combined with find_functions ~72% recall (per docs), vtable/function-pointer calls to undiscovered or unlifted targets become silent no-ops that corrupt control flow. The lifter assumes CTR already holds an OPD-resolved code address but nothing guarantees the preceding lifted code performed OPD resolution.
gaps.evidence: runtime/ppu/ppu_loader.cpp:114-143 (ps3_indirect_call returns on miss); docs/broad-testing-findings.md:89 (find_functions recall ~72%)

gaps.gap: Byte-reverse load/store (lwbrx/lhbrx/ldbrx/stwbrx/sthbrx) are lifted as raw host-order memcpy with NO bswap, relying on the host being little-endian and on the value being consumed in that same reversed convention. This is only correct on an LE host and is fragile: the value placed in the GPR is the host-native interpretation of the BE-stored bytes, which is correct for lXbrx semantics by accident of host endianness, but the in-code NOTE admits 'no bswap'. On a BE host it would be wrong, and mixing with vm_read* (which DO bswap) on the same address yields inconsistent values.

mtcrf ignores its field mask: both mtcr and mtcrf are lifted as ctx->cr = (uint32_t)gpr[rs], overwriting all 8 CR fields even when CRM selects a subset. The decoder distinguishes them (crm==0xFF -> mtcr) but the lifter collapses them.
gaps.evidence: ppu_lifter.py:799-800 (mtcr/mtcrf both full-register copy); decoder ppu_disasm.py:634-642

gaps.gap: mtfsf is an explicit no-op ('FPSCR update — ignored for now') and FPSCR rounding-mode/exception state is never modeled; fctiw/fctiwz/fctid/fctidz always use C default (round-toward-zero on truncation cast) regardless of FPSCR[RN], and frsp just casts to float. Vector status (VSCR) saturation flags are likewise not maintained by the saturating VMX handlers.
gaps.evidence: ppu_lifter.py:1075-1076 (mtfsf ignored); 883-896 (fctiw* via plain int cast)

The decode table is far larger than the set of implemented vector handlers (e.g. vsrab/vsrah, vsrh/vsrb, vrlh, vsum4*/vsumsws, vupkhsb/vupklsb/vupklsh, vpku*us/ss, vmuleub/vmulosb/vmulesh, vmhaddshs/vmhraddshs/vmladduhm/vmsumubm/vmsumuhm/vmsumuhs/vmsumshs/vmsumuhm, vavg* except vavgub, vctuxs edge cases). Each unimplemented op silently produces no state change.

gaps.gap: lvx/stvx force 16-byte alignment by masking EA (& ~0xF), which matches PPU hardware, but lvlx/lvrx and the element loads (lvebx/lvehx/lvewx) use unaligned byte loops; lvsl/lvsr are emitted but the generated permute vectors are only meaningful when paired with vperm, and there is no check that the disassembler-vs-lifter operand order for VA-form ops (vmaddfp/vnmsubfp/vmsum*) is consistent — the lifter hard-codes operand index assumptions (e.g. vmaddfp treats ops[2]=vB, ops[3]=vC) that must match the disasm emission exactly or lanes silently swap.

detect_functions() in the disassembler is a weak heuristic (prologue = mflr r0 + std/stw r0,X(r1); end at first blr) that cannot find leaf functions without a standard prologue, functions reached only by call-target/indirect analysis, or data-embedded code — the documented ~72% recall gap. The production lift relies entirely on an external --functions list, so any boundary error from find_functions/Ghidra propagates directly into wrong function ranges (and thus wrong mid-function tail-entry splits).

No game has booted end-to-end (project-acknowledged), and the PPU runtime reflects first-boot scaffolding rather than a correct executor: stuck-loop aborts, fabricated syscall returns, OOB-to-zero degradation, and unresolved-NID/indirect-call no-ops all keep execution 'progressing' at the cost of silent state divergence, making correctness bugs hard to localize.

code.area: SPU strategy (disasm, lift, runtime, channels, DMA, dynamic loading)
code.currentApproach:
ps3recomp pursues TWO parallel SPU strategies, and the code makes clear that #1 is the actually-wired production path while #2 is a built-but-not-integrated AOT pipeline.

(1) PPU-side fallback registry (the live strategy). The project does NOT execute SPU code in the shipping path. include/ps3emu/spu_fallback.h:6 states plainly "ps3recomp doesn't execute SPU code (no JIT for SPU ISA, no SPU LS model)." Instead, runtime/syscalls/spu_fallback.c implements a fixed 64-slot registry (SPU_FALLBACK_MAX=64, spu_fallback.c:15) keyed on the SPU image entry point. At sys_spu_thread_group_start (lv2_register.c:375) each thread's entry_point is looked up via spu_lookup_ppu_fallback; if a hand-written C handler is registered it runs on a host thread (Win32 CreateThread / pthread_create, lv2_register.c:405-417) and group_join blocks on it (lv2_register.c:467-492), collecting the worst (most-negative) exit status. If NO handler matches, the thread "completes instantly with status 0" (lv2_register.c:396-400) — i.e. the SPU job is silently a no-op returning CELL_OK. sys_spu_image_open (lv2_register.c:789) only parses the ELF header to extract e_entry and writes type=USER+entry into the guest sys_spu_image struct; it explicitly does NOT materialise segments/code (lv2_register.c:778-781). Each SPU thread gets a lazily-allocated virtual 256KB local store reachable from PPU via sys_spu_thread_write_ls/read_ls and from a fallback via spu_thread_get_local_store(tid) (lv2_register.c:751, spu_fallback.h:90).

(2) Static SPU->C recompilation pipeline (built, validated on one image, NOT wired into the build). Stages: extract_spu_images.py scans a PPU ELF/EBOOT for embedded big-endian EM_SPU(23) ELFs by ELF-magic search, computing each image size from max(end of section table, end of PT_LOAD) (extract_spu_images.py:62-82). find_spu_functions.py detects boundaries by seeding from e_entry + STT_FUNC symbols (exact when st_size>0) + ALL resolved branch targets brsl/brasl/br/bra/brz/brnz/brhz/brhnz (find_spu_functions.py:140-165), then walking forward until stop/stopd, `bi $r0` (SPU ABI return), an unconditional non-fallthrough branch, or the next seed (find_end, :191). spu_disasm.py decodes fixed 32-bit big-endian SPU instructions via opcode-width tables (RRR 4-bit, RI18 7-bit, RI16 9-bit, RI10 8-bit, RI8 10-bit, RR 11-bit, RI7 inside SPU_RR) rebuilt against RPCS3 SPUOpcodes.h; decode order is carefully sequenced (RI16 before RI10, channel ops before RI10) to resolve opcode-prefix collisions. spu_lifter.py emits one `void spu_func_XXXXXXXX(spu_context*)` per detected function, wiring ctx->gpr[N] (u128) to static-inline helpers in runtime/spu/spu_helpers.h; control flow uses goto for intra-function branches and tail-calls (ctx->pc=tgt; spu_func_tgt(ctx); return;) for cross-function, plus a fall-through tail-call chain (spu_lifter.py:225-229). brsl/brasl become direct C calls with link reg recovered from raw bits; `bi $r0` becomes a host `return;`; other indirect branches (bi/bisl/biz...) set ctx->pc and call spu_indirect_branch. It emits a spu_function_table[] + spu_recomp_register(). Runtime glue (spu_channels.c) implements spu_rdch/wrch/rchcnt routing MFC channels to a per-context mfc_engine (8-slot registry) and mailbox/signal/event/decrementer/SRR0 to spu_context fields; spu_indirect_branch does a linear scan over a 65536-entry flat registry filtered by image_id (spu_channels.c:171-194), halting with a diagnostic on miss. DMA (spu_dma.h) executes synchronously: mfc_submit immediately memcpy's between LS and vm_base+EA (mfc_do_transfer:118), all tags reported complete instantly. wrap_spu_elf.py builds minimal SPU ELFs for the 4 integration tests. Helpers are unit-tested (63 cases) and the lifter was run end-to-end on one image (Uncharted: Drake's Fortune SPU blob).
strengths: Disassembler is grounded in an authoritative source (RPCS3 SPUOpcodes.h) and the decode-order collisions (RI16-before-RI10, channel-ops-before-RI10, RI7-as-RR) are documented with the exact opcode clashes they prevent (spu_disasm.py:99-128, :388-407). The prior buggy tables were caught and rewritten — a real correctness recovery documented in SPU_LIFTER.md:160-187.

Single source of truth for semantics: all per-instruction helpers live in runtime/spu/spu_helpers.h, shared by the lifter, runtime, and a 63-case unit suite (test_spu_helpers.c). This is good engineering hygiene and made the endianness bug fixable in one place.

The host little-endian sub-lane hazard for SPU big-endian element order is explicitly understood and handled at the LS<->register boundary (spu_ls_read128/write128 per-lane byte-swap, spu_context.h:199-234) and in the mpy/xsbh sub-lane indexing (spu_helpers.h:58-70, :198-212), with comments. Found via the DMA integration test.
shufb faithfully implements the 0x80/0xC0/0xE0 special selectors per Cell BE ISA (spu_helpers.h:109-127), and selb is bit-exact.

Function-boundary detection is pragmatic for stripped images: seeding from branch targets (not just calls) jumped detected functions 44->461 on the real image, and unresolved cross-function targets get auto-generated indirect-dispatch stubs so the link always succeeds (spu_lifter.py:542-552).

The fallback registry is a clean, documented escape hatch for games that genuinely need SPU output (decompressors/mixers/physics), with real host-thread concurrency and proper group_join blocking + worst-status semantics (lv2_register.c:467-492).
image_id support in the dispatch registry anticipates SPURS overlay loading (kernel/policy/job at overlapping LS addresses), spu_context.h:127-131, spu_channels.c:171-182.

gaps.gap: The shipping SPU strategy is to NOT run SPU code: any SPU thread group with no registered fallback completes instantly with exit status 0 (CELL_OK), silently. PPU code that depends on SPU-produced data reads garbage/stale memory. This is the project's central admitted limitation and applies to every game unless a per-job hand-written handler exists.

The fallback path is fully MANUAL and per-job: a human must reverse-engineer each SPU job, hard-code its entry point (read from a [SPU] image_open log line), and re-implement its output in C. It does not scale across games and cannot handle non-trivial jobs (the doc itself flags decompressors/mixers/physics as hard to hand-write). Registry is also a hard cap of 64 entries.

The automated SPU->C lifting pipeline is NOT wired into the build. SPU_LIFTER.md lists 'Wire spu_lifter.py into the build alongside ppu_lifter.py (CMake)' as still-open, so the general path that would actually execute SPU code is not part of any produced executable.
gaps.evidence: docs/SPU_LIFTER.md:261 ('Wire spu_lifter.py into the build ... (CMake)' under TODO §4)

gaps.gap: Statically lifting SPU is undermined by dynamic loading: SPU code is routinely DMA'd/overlaid into local store at runtime (SPURS kernel/policy/job), so the set of functions present statically in an extracted image is incomplete. The pipeline only handles images found by ELF-magic scan of the PPU binary; code uploaded via sys_spu_thread_write_ls or job descriptors is invisible to extract_spu_images.py. This is acknowledged in the project's own known-gaps.
gaps.evidence: tools/extract_spu_images.py:5-13 (only finds embedded ELFs); spu_context.h:127-131 (image overlap acknowledged); project KNOWN GAPS: 'SPU code is often dynamically loaded into local store (hard to find statically)'

gaps.gap: MFC DMA is fully synchronous and ignores fences/barriers, tags, and atomics. mfc_submit memcpy's immediately and marks all tags complete; barrier/eieio/sync are no-ops; MFC_RdAtomicStat always returns 0 (PUTLLC success) and there is no GETLLAR/PUTLLC/PUTLLUC reservation model at all. SPU atomic lock-line semantics (used by SPURS synchronization) are not modeled, so concurrent fallback host-threads against the same lock line would not behave like hardware.
gaps.evidence: runtime/spu/spu_dma.h:118-145 (immediate memcpy), :225-230 (barrier no-op), :338-342 (atomic always success); no MFC_GETLLAR/PUTLLC opcode handling anywhere

gaps.gap: DMA list (PUTL/GETL) stall-and-notify is silently dropped, and list transfers advance spu->mfc_lsa as a side effect (clobbering the channel-staged LSA) with no notify event raised. Games using stall-and-notify list DMA would diverge.
gaps.evidence: runtime/spu/spu_dma.h:152-186 (stall_notify computed but the branch body is empty, :179-182; mfc_lsa mutated :177)

gaps.gap: Halt-on-condition instructions (hgt/hlgt/heq/hgti/hlgti/heqi) and stopd are lifted as no-ops/plain stop — recompiled code does not honor SPU halt/trap semantics, so a job relying on a conditional halt for control flow or error signaling silently continues.

No FPSCR / floating-point status model. fscrrd returns zero (stub) and fscrwr is unhandled; SPU FP is computed with host IEEE semantics (no SPU-specific denorm-flush, no NaN/extended-range single-precision quirks, reciprocal/rsqrt estimates use exact host math). frest/frsqest are exact 1/x and 1/sqrt rather than the hardware estimate+Newton-step pairs, so bit-exact divergence vs real SPU is expected for FP-heavy jobs.
gaps.evidence: runtime/spu/spu_helpers.h:187 (spu_fscrrd returns spu_zero), :205 (frsqest exact), :67-68 (fi Newton approximation); docs/SPU_LIFTER.md:113-114, :151-152

gaps.gap: mfspr is a stub returning 0 and SPU SPRs are not modeled; mtspr is not lifted at all. Any job reading/writing SPU special-purpose registers gets wrong values.

Indirect-branch dispatch (spu_indirect_branch) is a pure static-target lookup: it can only land on an address that the boundary detector promoted to a registered spu_func_*. Computed jumps into the MIDDLE of a function, or into dynamically uploaded code, halt with SPU_STATUS_STOPPED_BY_HALT. Switch tables / function pointers / vtable dispatch in SPU code are therefore unresolved — the same indirect-branch problem the project flags for PPU. Lookup is also an O(n) linear scan over up to 65536 entries per indirect branch.
gaps.evidence: runtime/spu/spu_channels.c:171-194 (linear scan, halt on miss); tools/spu_lifter.py:459-478 (bi/bisl/biz -> spu_indirect_branch)

gaps.gap: Double-precision float family is entirely unlifted. dfa/dfs/dfm/dfma/dfms/dfnms/dfnma/dfceq/dfcgt/dfcmeq/dfcmgt/dfsv/fesd/frds are decoded by the disassembler (SPU_RR) but have NO entry in the lifter's dispatch tables and NO helper — they fall through to a `/* TODO spu: ... */` no-op that does not write rt. Any double-precision SPU math silently produces no result.
gaps.evidence: tools/spu_lifter.py:484-486 (fallthrough TODO); rr_bin/rr_un tables :297-342 omit all df* and fesd/frds; spu_helpers.h has no df* helpers; SPU_LIFTER.md:152 lists double-precision as Future/not-hit

gaps.gap: The lifter's correctness on real images is unverified: SPU_LIFTER.md states the only end-to-end real run (Uncharted entry function) 'happens to be pure setup with no PPU dependency ... zero channel I/O', and the planned diff-vs-RPCS3 trace converter is 'still to be written'. So beyond 4 hand-written micro-tests and 63 helper unit cases, there is no evidence lifted output is behaviorally correct against hardware/RPCS3.
gaps.evidence: docs/SPU_LIFTER.md:244-245 (entry fn pure setup, zero channel I/O), :289 (converter still to be written), :308-309

gaps.gap: brhz/brhnz and biz/binz halfword conditions use a hardcoded 'preferred halfword' lane (_u16[1]) whose correctness on the LE host is explicitly flagged as unresolved; shlqby direction is likewise listed as still-open. These are exercised by real branch-heavy SPU code and could mis-predict branches.
gaps.evidence: tools/spu_lifter.py:494 (half = _u16[1] with comment); docs/SPU_LIFTER.md:212-216 (shlqby direction + preferred-halfword 'Still open')

gaps.gap: sys_spu_image_open never materialises SPU segments and many SPU syscalls route to sys_spu_thread_stub which blindly returns CELL_OK (gpr[3]=0). Combined with the no-op job execution, the entire SPU subsystem can report success to the PPU while doing nothing.

args_size passed to fallback handlers is always 0 (the syscall API doesn't carry it), so a handler cannot know its descriptor size without out-of-band knowledge; documented but a real ergonomic/correctness limitation for generic fallbacks.

The RI7 quad shift/rotate forms (shlqbyi/rotqbyi/shlqbii/rotqbii) are mis-decoded by the disassembler as 3-register RR ops and the lifter recovers the i7 immediate by string-stripping the spurious '$r' prefix — a fragile cross-module workaround rather than fixing the decoder, acknowledged as a 'disassembler quirk'.

verified.claim: N64Recomp emits one C function per guest function with signature taking (uint8_t* rdram, recomp_context* ctx), translating instructions literally (e.g. addiu $r4,$r4,0x20 -> ctx->r4 = ADD32(ctx->r4, 0x20)), and converting jalr indirect calls to LOOKUP_FUNC(ctx->r25)(rdram, ctx) and relocated lui to RELOC_HI16(...) macros.
verified.explanation:
Every component of this claim is supported by N64Recomp's primary sources (official README and the recompiler source in src/cgenerator.cpp and src/main.cpp).

(1) One C function per guest function with the stated signature: CONFIRMED. The README states the recompiler splits the input binary into functions "that are each individually recompiled into a C function." The code generator's emit_function_start in src/cgenerator.cpp emits exactly "RECOMP_FUNC void {}(uint8_t* rdram, recomp_context* ctx) {{", and src/main.cpp emits the matching prototypes as "void {}(uint8_t* rdram, recomp_context* ctx);". So the (uint8_t* rdram, recomp_context* ctx) parameter pair is exact and correct (return type is void, with a RECOMP_FUNC attribute macro on the definition — a detail the claim omits but does not contradict).

(2) Literal/per-instruction translation with the addiu/ADD32 example: CONFIRMED VERBATIM. The README gives this exact example: "the instruction addiu $r4, $r4, 0x20 ... gets recompiled into ctx->r4 = ADD32(ctx->r4, 0X20);". The README also describes the process as instructions being "processed one-by-one and corresponding C code emitted as each one gets processed," matching "translating instructions literally." The generator maps BinaryOpType::Add32 to the "ADD32" macro string.

(3) jalr -> LOOKUP_FUNC(ctx->r25)(rdram, ctx): CONFIRMED VERBATIM. The README states "the instruction jalr $25 would get recompiled as LOOKUP_FUNC(ctx->r25)(rdram, ctx);". The generator emits the LOOKUP_FUNC(...)(rdram, ctx) form (for direct/known-address indirect calls it emits a literal address; for register-based jalr it uses the register operand, i.e. ctx->r25).

(4) Relocated lui -> RELOC_HI16(...): CONFIRMED. Verified against the primary source: N64Recomp/include/recomp.h on the main branch (repo last pushed 2026-05-27). The macro definitions read verbatim:

The claim is overwhelmingly accurate against primary source (XenonUtils/ppc_context.h and the project README), with one genuine imprecision in the indexing formula.

CONFIRMED — Function signature. The header defines verbatim: `#define PPC_FUNC(x) void x(PPCContext& __restrict ctx, uint8_t* base)`, plus `typedef void PPCFunc(struct PPCContext& __restrict__ ctx, uint8_t* base);`. The README corroborates that CPU state (a PPCContext with all PPC registers) is passed to every PPC function, and the second argument is the base pointer because the Xbox 360 uses 32-bit pointers. So "every recompiled guest function has this signature" is true (the recompiler emits all guest functions through PPC_FUNC; PPC_FUNC_IMPL = `extern "C" PPC_FUNC(x)` and PPC_EXTERN_FUNC = `extern PPC_FUNC(x)` are the same signature).

CONFIRMED — Indirect calls via PPC_LOOKUP_FUNC dereferencing a function-pointer table. Verbatim: `#define PPC_LOOKUP_FUNC(x, y) *(PPCFunc**)(x + PPC_IMAGE_BASE + PPC_IMAGE_SIZE + (uint64_t(uint32_t(y) - PPC_CODE_BASE) * 2))` and `#define PPC_CALL_INDIRECT_FUNC(x) (PPC_LOOKUP_FUNC(base, x))(ctx, base)`. It dereferences a PPCFunc** table — correct.

CONFIRMED — Stored just past the XEX region in the base allocation. The macro computes the address as `base + PPC_IMAGE_BASE + PPC_IMAGE_SIZE + ...` (i.e., immediately after the loaded image), and the README says function addresses are "placed after the valid XEX memory region in the base memory pointer," exported via macros in ppc_config.h.

CONFIRMED — Replaced an earlier 8GB virtual allocation. README verbatim: "This was previously implemented by creating an 8 GB virtual allocation, but it had too much memory pressure. Now it relies on function addresses being placed after the valid XEX memory region in the base memory pointer." (The claim's word "sparse" is a reasonable characterization of a large lazily/over-committed virtual allocation, though the README itself just says "8 GB virtual allocation.")

IMPRECISE — "indexed by guest address*2." The actual table index is `(uint64_t(uint32_t(y) - PPC_CODE_BASE) * 2)`, i.e., (guest_address − PPC_CODE_BASE) * 2, not raw guest_address * 2. The *2 scaling factor is correct (two-byte spacing per 4-byte guest instruction, since the smallest instruction alignment is 4 and entries are spaced by addr/2... effectively one 8-byte pointer slot per 4 bytes of code via the *2 on a code base offset). The README does loosely say "original instruction address multiplied by 2," which matches the claim's wording, but the precise index subtracts PPC_CODE_BASE first so the table is relative to the start of the code region, not the absolute guest address. This is the one part that is exaggerated/imprecise rather than exactly true.

Supporting context (prior art / siblings): N64Recomp uses the analogous pattern with a different argument ORDER — `LOOKUP_FUNC(ctx->r25)(rdram, ctx)` (rdram/base first, then context) and the runtime maintains a loaded-section table for lookups, whereas XenonRecomp puts ctx first then base and uses the perfect-hash table embedded in the base allocation. UnleashedRecomp is the runtime/HLE layer that consumes XenonRecomp output and supplies host implementations (hookable via the weak-linking PPC_FUNC_IMPL/PPC_FUNC aliasing pattern); XenosRecomp is the companion GPU shader recompiler. These do not change the verdict on the core claim.

Net: 4 of the 5 components are confirmed verbatim from primary source; only the indexing description (raw address*2 vs (address − PPC_CODE_BASE)*2) is imprecise — hence partially-true rather than fully confirmed.

1) Byteswap via __builtin_bswap16/32/64 inside the macros — CONFIRMED, verbatim from XenonUtils/ppc_context.h (two independent raw-file reads agree exactly):
   #define PPC_LOAD_U16(x) __builtin_bswap16(*(volatile uint16_t*)(base + (x)))
   #define PPC_LOAD_U32(x) __builtin_bswap32(*(volatile uint32_t*)(base + (x)))
   #define PPC_LOAD_U64(x) __builtin_bswap64(*(volatile uint64_t*)(base + (x)))
   #define PPC_STORE_U16(x, y) *(volatile uint16_t*)(base + (x)) = __builtin_bswap16(y)
   #define PPC_STORE_U32(x, y) *(volatile uint32_t*)(base + (x)) = __builtin_bswap32(y)
   #define PPC_STORE_U64(x, y) *(volatile uint64_t*)(base + (x)) = __builtin_bswap64(y)
   PRECISION NOTE: The claim's "16/32/64" enumeration is correct and notably accurate because the 8-bit cases are NOT byteswapped (PPC_LOAD_U8 / PPC_STORE_U8 have no bswap, as a single byte needs none). So the claim correctly omits an 8-bit bswap.

2) volatile-qualified — CONFIRMED. Every load/store macro casts through (volatile uintN_t*).

3) "specifically to stop Clang from unsafe reordering" — CONFIRMED as the project's own stated rationale. README, verbatim: "All the memory loads and stores are marked volatile to prevent Clang from doing unsafe code reordering." This is the documented motivation, not merely the fact-checker's inference. (Caveat on framing, not truth: README says "Clang" specifically because the recompiled output is built with Clang; volatile semantics constrain reordering for any conforming compiler, so the rationale is real but the wording reflects the project's target toolchain.)

4) Vector registers stored fully byte-reversed (16 bytes) rather than per-lane swapped — CONFIRMED. README, verbatim: "Instead of swapping individual 32-bit elements, the recompiler chooses to reverse the entire 16-byte vector." The README further notes the consequences (instructions compensate via reversed component accessors, e.g. WZY vs XYZ, and reversed pack arguments), consistent with whole-vector reversal rather than per-lane/per-element swap.

CONTEXT (supporting analysis on related projects): The general endianness-handling pattern is shared design heritage. N64Recomp (prior art by the same broader ecosystem / Mr-Wiseguy) established the static-recompilation-to-C++ approach with similar host/guest endianness bridging. UnleashedRecomp is the runtime/HLE consumer of XenonRecomp's output and is built with Clang (which is why the README phrases the volatile rationale around Clang). XenosRecomp is the sibling GPU shader recompiler (different domain — DXBC/shader translation — not the CPU memory macros in question). These corroborate the toolchain context but the load-bearing evidence for the claim is XenonRecomp's own header and README.

Overall: the claim is accurate on all four assertions. The only refinements are (a) 8-bit accesses are deliberately not swapped (the claim's "16/32/64" wording already reflects this), and (b) "specifically to stop Clang" mirrors the README's exact wording, which is tied to the project's Clang-based output rather than implying volatile only affects Clang.

UnleashedRecomp binds Xbox kernel imports to host C++ via GUEST_FUNCTION_HOOK(__imp__Name, HostFn) expanding to PPC_FUNC(__imp__Name){ HostToGuestFunction<HostFn>(ctx, base); }, with ArgTranslator marshalling integer args from r3..r10, float args from f1..f13, and returns into r3 (int/ptr) or f1 (float).
verified.explanation:
Every element of this claim is verified verbatim against the canonical primary source (hedge-dev/UnleashedRecomp, UnleashedRecomp/kernel/function.h, and hedge-dev/XenonRecomp, XenonUtils/ppc_context.h).

1) MACRO EXPANSION — EXACT MATCH. function.h defines:
  #define GUEST_FUNCTION_HOOK(subroutine, function) \
      PPC_FUNC(subroutine) { HostToGuestFunction<function>(ctx, base); }
This is exactly the claimed expansion. PPC_FUNC is defined in XenonRecomp's ppc_context.h as: #define PPC_FUNC(x) void x(PPCContext& __restrict ctx, uint8_t* base) — so PPC_FUNC(__imp__Name) yields a function taking (ctx, base), matching the claim. (Minor pedantic note: the real signature uses __restrict and passes uint8_t* base; the claim's shorthand omits __restrict, but this is immaterial.)

2) __imp__ NAMING — CONFIRMED. UnleashedRecomp/kernel/imports.cpp uses the hook exactly as claimed, e.g. GUEST_FUNCTION_HOOK(__imp__XNotifyGetNext, XNotifyGetNext); GUEST_FUNCTION_HOOK(__imp__NtCreateFile, NtCreateFile); etc. The first argument is the guest import thunk symbol (__imp__Name), the second is the native host C++ function — exactly the host/HLE binding the claim describes.

3) INTEGER ARGS r3..r10 — CONFIRMED. ArgTranslator::GetIntegerArgumentValue returns ctx.r3..ctx.r10 for arg indices 0..7 (8 GPRs: r3,r4,r5,r6,r7,r8,r9,r10), then spills to the stack (base + r1 + 0x54 + (arg-8)*8) for args >= 8. So integer args are marshalled from r3..r10 as claimed (with stack overflow handling the claim doesn't mention but doesn't contradict). Note it reads the .u32 field.

4) FLOAT ARGS f1..f13 — CONFIRMED. ArgTranslator::GetPrecisionArgumentValue returns ctx.f1..ctx.f13 for indices 0..12 (13 FPRs: f1 through f13), reading .f64. Matches the claim exactly.

5) RETURN VALUES r3 (int/ptr) / f1 (float) — CONFIRMED. In HostToGuestFunction<Func>: pointer returns write ctx.r3.u64 (host->guest-relative offset); is_precise_v (float/double) returns write ctx.f1.f64; otherwise (integral) ctx.r3.u64 = (uint64_t)v. So int and pointer returns go to r3, float/double returns go to f1 — exactly as claimed. (GuestToHostFunction, the reverse direction, symmetrically reads results from r3/f1.)

This matches the PowerPC EABI / Xbox 360 Xenon calling convention (GPRs r3-r10 for the first 8 integer/pointer args, FPRs f1-f13 for float args, r3 for integer/pointer return, f1 for FP return), which is what UnleashedRecomp implements.

PRECISION CAVEATS (claim is accurate, but to be exact): (a) ArgTranslator is defined in UnleashedRecomp itself (kernel/function.h), not in the generic XenonRecomp recompiler — XenonRecomp only provides PPC_FUNC and the PPCContext register layout. The arg-marshalling/ABI glue is part of the Unleashed runtime/HLE layer, which is consistent with the claim attributing it to UnleashedRecomp. (b) Argument-to-register ordinal mapping is per-type-stream: integer and float arguments are assigned independent ordinals (floatOrdinal for floats; integers use positional index), so e.g. f1 = first float arg, r3 = first integer/pointer arg, rather than a single interleaved sequence — the claim's r3..r10 / f1..f13 framing is correct at this level of detail. The claim is fully supported by primary sources with no exaggeration.

verified.claim: XenonAnalyse detects jump tables primarily by recognizing the `mtctr r0` instruction followed by `bctr`, and emits the resolved tables to a separate TOML file (e.g. SWA_switch_tables.toml) that XenonRecomp consumes to generate native C++ switch/goto.
verified.explanation:
All four parts of the claim are supported by primary sources (the hedge-dev/XenonRecomp repository README, source code, and the UnleashedRecomp SWA.toml config).

1) Detection via mtctr/bctr — CONFIRMED (with one nuance). The XenonRecomp README states verbatim: "The typical way to find jump tables is by searching for the `mtctr r0` instruction. It will almost always be followed with a `bctr`, with the previous instructions computing the jump address." The actual implementation in XenonAnalyse/main.cpp confirms this: it uses SearchMask() to match instruction-sequence patterns that all terminate in `PPC_INST_MTCTR, PPC_INST_BCTR` (e.g. the absolute-switch pattern "PPC_INST_LIS, PPC_INST_ADDI, PPC_INST_RLWINM, PPC_INST_LWZX, PPC_INST_MTCTR, PPC_INST_BCTR", plus computed/offset/word-offset variants), then ScanTable()/ReadTable() resolve the targets. Nuance: the code matches the full instruction-pattern sequence ending in MTCTR+BCTR; it is not literally keyed on the register being "r0" specifically (no explicit r0 check appears in the matching code). "mtctr r0 followed by bctr" is the README's simplified human description of the real pattern-sequence matcher. So the spirit/mechanism is exactly right; the "r0" detail is a documentation simplification rather than a hardcoded register filter.

2) Separate TOML output — CONFIRMED. The README documents XenonAnalyse's CLI as "XenonAnalyse [input XEX file path] [output jump table TOML file path]" and main.cpp emits "[[switch]]" entries (base, r, default, labels) and writes them to a standalone file (std::ofstream f(argv[2])). The example filename SWA_switch_tables.toml is real: UnleashedRecompLib/config/SWA.toml contains `switch_table_file_path = "SWA_switch_tables.toml"`.

3) XenonRecomp consumes it — CONFIRMED. The README documents the config key: "switch_table_file_path - Path to the TOML file containing the jump table definitions. The recompiler uses this file to convert jump tables to real switch cases."

4) Generates native C++ switch + goto — CONFIRMED. XenonRecomp/recompiler.cpp literally emits a C++ switch statement whose cases use goto-to-label: it prints `switch ({}.u64) {`, then for each label `case {}:` followed by `goto loc_{:X};` (with out-of-bounds cases emitting an error/return and a `default: __builtin_unreachable();`). So "switch/goto" is precisely accurate.

Overall: the claim is accurate. The only thing to flag as a minor over-precision is the literal "r0" — detection is pattern-sequence based ending in mtctr+bctr rather than a hardcoded r0 register check, but the README itself phrases it as "mtctr r0," so the claim faithfully reflects the documentation.
